#| label: render-env-helpers

# Render numeric comparison tables at the full text width without scaling type.
r2_full_width_table <- function(data, digits = 1, font_size = 9, first_column_width = NULL, col.names = NULL, escape = TRUE) {
    if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
        table <- knitr::kable(
            data,
            col.names = if (is.null(col.names)) colnames(data) else col.names,
            escape = escape,
            digits = digits, row.names = FALSE,
            format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = FALSE
        ) |>
            kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = font_size) |>
            kableExtra::row_spec(0:nrow(data), color = "black")
        if (!is.null(first_column_width)) {
            table <- kableExtra::column_spec(table, 1, width = first_column_width)
        }
        table_attributes <- attributes(table)
        table <- sub(
            "\\begin{tabular}{",
            "\\begin{tabular*}{\\linewidth}{@{\\extracolsep{\\fill}}",
            as.character(table),
            fixed = TRUE
        )
        table <- sub("\\end{tabular}", "\\end{tabular*}", table, fixed = TRUE)
        attributes(table) <- table_attributes
        table
    } else if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
        knitr::kable(
            data,
            col.names = if (is.null(col.names)) colnames(data) else col.names,
            escape = escape,
            digits = digits, row.names = FALSE, format = "html",
            table.attr = 'style="width: 100%;"'
        ) |>
            kableExtra::kable_styling(full_width = TRUE) |>
            kableExtra::row_spec(0:nrow(data), color = "black")
    } else {
        knitr::kable(data, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE, format = "pipe")
    }
}

# Pre-load regional data for abstract inline references
# This code runs before the abstract to provide numbers for inline R code
library(jsonlite)

# ── Census year configuration ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Change this single value to switch all output paths between census years.
# All output data is read from: ../output/{region}/{census_year}/{file}
census_year <- "2022"
r2_results_dir <- "../results/model"
r2_reporting_dir <- "../results/model"
r2_gravity_parameters <- read.csv("../data/parameters/distance_frequency_wide.csv", check.names = FALSE)
r2_gravity_beta <- setNames(r2_gravity_parameters$beta, r2_gravity_parameters[["NPT purpose"]])
stopifnot(
    !anyDuplicated(names(r2_gravity_beta)),
    all(c("Commuting", "Shopping", "Social", "Leisure") %in% names(r2_gravity_beta)),
    all(is.finite(r2_gravity_beta)), all(r2_gravity_beta < 0)
)
r2_beta <- function(profile) sprintf("%.7f", r2_gravity_beta[[profile]])
r2_metrics <- fromJSON(file.path(r2_results_dir, "national_metrics.json"))
r2_oa_counts <- read.csv(file.path(r2_results_dir, "oa_counts.csv"))
r2_sensitivity <- read.csv(file.path(r2_reporting_dir, "sensitivity.csv"))
r2_sensitivity <- subset(r2_sensitivity, family %in% c(
    "AP band", "Decay multiplier", "Purpose-weight multiplier"
))
r2_scenario_totals <- aggregate(cbind(
    baseline_volume, potential_volume, immediate_volume,
    conditional_volume
) ~ family + scenario, r2_sensitivity, sum)
r2_scenario_totals$potential_pct <- 100 * r2_scenario_totals$potential_volume /
    r2_scenario_totals$baseline_volume
r2_scenario_totals$immediate_pct <- 100 * r2_scenario_totals$immediate_volume /
    r2_scenario_totals$baseline_volume
r2_envelope <- range(r2_scenario_totals$potential_pct)
r2_pct <- function(volume) sprintf("%.1f", 100 * volume / r2_metrics$baseline_volume)

# Helper: construct output path for a region and file
opath <- function(region, file = "") {
    if (file == "adoption_propensity_categorized.gpkg") {
        result <- file.path("../data/areas", paste0(region, ".gpkg"))
    } else if (file == "enhanced_charging_infrastructure.gpkg") {
        result <- file.path("../data/charging", paste0(region, ".gpkg"))
    } else if (file == "propensity_group_analysis_biplot.png") {
        result <- file.path("figures", paste0("demographic_biplot_", region, ".png"))
    } else {
        result <- file.path("../results/model/regions", region, file)
    }
    stopifnot(file.exists(result))
    result
}

regions_abstract <- c("HITRANS", "Nestrans", "SESTRAN", "SPT", "SWESTRANS", "Tactran", "ZetTrans")

regional_data_abstract <- list()

for (region in regions_abstract) {
    file_path <- opath(region, paste0(region, "_comprehensive_summary.json"))
    if (file.exists(file_path)) {
        regional_data_abstract[[region]] <- fromJSON(file_path)
    } else {
        warning(paste("File not found:", file_path))

}

# Calculate totals for abstract

        val <- x$conversion_potential$total_baseline_trips
        if (is.null(val)) {
            return(0)
        }
        return(as.numeric(val))
    }), na.rm = TRUE),
    total_conversion = sum(sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
        val <- x$conversion_potential$total_baseline_trips
        if (is.null(val)) {
            return(0)
        }
        return(as.numeric(val))
    }), na.rm = TRUE),
    immediately_feasible = sum(sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
        val <- x$immediately_feasible_trips
        if (is.null(val)) {
            return(0)
        }
        return(as.numeric(val))
    }), na.rm = TRUE),
    constrained_unlockable = sum(sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
        val <- x$constrained_unlockable_trips
        if (is.null(val)) {
            return(0)
        }
        return(as.numeric(val))
    }), na.rm = TRUE),
    additional_from_charging = 0 # placeholder, computed below from constrained_unlockable * unlock_factor
)

# Verify data loaded
if (length(regional_data_abstract) == 0) {
    warning("No regional data loaded for abstract calculations!")
}

# Compute additional_from_charging correctly: constrained_unlockable * unlock_factor
# The JSON field additional_trips_from_charging is stale (computed from pre-integration
# constrained_unlockable_trips, but the JSON stores the post-integration value).
# Recompute from the consistent constrained_unlockable total.
scoring_weights_abstract <- fromJSON("../data/parameters/scoring_weights.json")
unlock_factor_abstract <- 1 # Conditional restoration of the capacity-constrained tier, not uptake.
if (!is.null(unlock_factor_abstract)) {
    abstract_totals$additional_from_charging <- abstract_totals$constrained_unlockable * unlock_factor_abstract
} else {
    abstract_totals$additional_from_charging <- 0
}

abstract_totals$total_convertible <- sum(sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
    val <- x$conversion_potential$total_baseline_trips
    if (is.null(val)) {
        return(0)
    }
    return(as.numeric(val))
}), na.rm = TRUE)

abstract_totals$total_final_conversion_potential <- sum(sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
    val <- x$conversion_potential$final_conversion_potential
    if (is.null(val)) {
        return(0)
    }
    return(as.numeric(val))
}), na.rm = TRUE)

abstract_totals$conversion_rate <- (abstract_totals$total_final_conversion_potential / abstract_totals$total_convertible) * 100

# Calculate weighted average percentages using pre-calculated values from executive_summary
# These percentages are relative to convertible trips and sum to 100%
total_convertible_for_weights <- sum(sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
    val <- x$conversion_potential$final_conversion_potential
    if (is.null(val)) {
        return(0)
    }
    return(as.numeric(val))
}), na.rm = TRUE)

abstract_totals$immediately_pct <- sum(sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
    pct <- x$executive_summary$immediately_feasible_pct
    weight <- x$conversion_potential$final_conversion_potential
    if (is.null(pct) || is.null(weight)) {
        return(0)
    }
    return(as.numeric(pct) * as.numeric(weight))
}), na.rm = TRUE) / total_convertible_for_weights

abstract_totals$constrained_pct <- sum(sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
    pct <- x$executive_summary$constrained_unlockable_pct
    weight <- x$conversion_potential$final_conversion_potential
    if (is.null(pct) || is.null(weight)) {
        return(0)
    }
    return(as.numeric(pct) * as.numeric(weight))
}), na.rm = TRUE) / total_convertible_for_weights

abstract_totals$infeasible_trips <- sum(sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
    val <- x$currently_infeasible_trips
    if (is.null(val)) {
        return(0)
    }
    return(as.numeric(val))
}), na.rm = TRUE) / abstract_totals$total_convertible * 100

# additional_from_charging already correctly computed above from constrained_unlockable * unlock_factor

abstract_totals$total_commute_trip <- sum(sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
    val <- x$purpose_replacement_analysis$Commuting$baseline_trips

}), na.rm = TRUE)

    return(as.numeric(val))
}), na.rm = TRUE)

abstract_totals$commute_replacement_rate <- (abstract_totals$total_replaceable_commute_trip / abstract_totals$total_commute_trip) * 100

abstract_totals$total_shopping_trip <- sum(sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
    val <- x$purpose_replacement_analysis$shopping$baseline_trips
    if (is.null(val)) {
        return(0)
    }
    return(as.numeric(val))
}), na.rm = TRUE)

abstract_totals$total_replaceable_shopping_trip <- sum(sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
    val <- x$purpose_replacement_analysis$shopping$replaceable_trips
    if (is.null(val)) {
        return(0)
    }
    return(as.numeric(val))
}), na.rm = TRUE)

abstract_totals$shopping_replacement_rate <- (abstract_totals$total_replaceable_shopping_trip / abstract_totals$total_shopping_trip) * 100

# Calculate trip weights for weighted averages
trip_weights_abstract <- sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
    val <- x$conversion_potential$total_baseline_trips

    }

})

# Use weighted.mean for constraint calculations (weighted by trip volume)
abstract_totals$range_constraint <- weighted.mean(

        if (is.null(val)) {

        return(as.numeric(val))

abstract_totals$two_seater_pct <- mean(sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
    val <- x$executive_summary$ev_type_breakdown$two_seater_pct

abstract_totals$four_seater_pct <- mean(sapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) {
    val <- x$executive_summary$ev_type_breakdown$four_seater_pct

    return(as.numeric(val))

ratio_two_seater_four_seater <- abstract_totals$two_seater_pct / abstract_totals$four_seater_pct

# Calculate top 3 and last trip purposes for abstract
all_purposes_abstract <- unique(unlist(lapply(regional_data_abstract, function(x) names(x$purpose_replacement_analysis))))

purpose_rates_abstract <- data.frame(
    purpose = character(),
    replacement_rate = numeric(),
    replaceable_volume = numeric(),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (purpose in all_purposes_abstract) {
    total_trips <- 0
    replaceable_trips <- 0

    for (x in regional_data_abstract) {
        if (!is.null(x$purpose_replacement_analysis) && purpose %in% names(x$purpose_replacement_analysis)) {
            purpose_data <- x$purpose_replacement_analysis[[purpose]]
            total_trips <- total_trips + as.numeric(ifelse(is.null(purpose_data$baseline_trips), 0, purpose_data$baseline_trips))
            replaceable_trips <- replaceable_trips + as.numeric(ifelse(is.null(purpose_data$replaceable_trips), 0, purpose_data$replaceable_trips))
        }
    }

    if (total_trips > 0) {
        # Cap replacement rate at 100% (cannot replace more trips than exist)
        purpose_rates_abstract <- rbind(
            purpose_rates_abstract,
            data.frame(
                purpose = purpose,
                replacement_rate = min(100, (replaceable_trips / total_trips) * 100),
                replaceable_volume = replaceable_trips
            )
        )
    }
}

purpose_rates_abstract <- purpose_rates_abstract[order(-purpose_rates_abstract$replacement_rate), ]

# Rank absolute volume separately from substitution rates.
volume_purposes_abstract <- purpose_rates_abstract[order(-purpose_rates_abstract$replaceable_volume), ]

# Extract top 3 and last
abstract_totals$top1_purpose <- purpose_rates_abstract$purpose[1]
abstract_totals$top1_rate <- purpose_rates_abstract$replacement_rate[1]
abstract_totals$top2_purpose <- purpose_rates_abstract$purpose[2]
abstract_totals$top2_rate <- purpose_rates_abstract$replacement_rate[2]
abstract_totals$top3_purpose <- purpose_rates_abstract$purpose[3]
abstract_totals$top3_rate <- purpose_rates_abstract$replacement_rate[3]
abstract_totals$last_purpose <- purpose_rates_abstract$purpose[nrow(purpose_rates_abstract)]
abstract_totals$last_rate <- purpose_rates_abstract$replacement_rate[nrow(purpose_rates_abstract)]

# Calculate four-seater to two-seater ratio
abstract_totals$four_to_two_ratio <- abstract_totals$four_seater_pct / abstract_totals$two_seater_pct

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Transport decarbonisation requires spatial assessment of where EV adoption is feasible, not merely whether nominal range is sufficient, but whether demographic readiness, infrastructure provision, and trip characteristics are jointly satisfied. Low-cost, short-range (frugal) EVs represent an affordability-oriented segment that may address equity gaps left by premium EVs, yet their spatial viability has not been systematically assessed at trip level. This study integrates census-based adoption propensity, purpose-specific suitability, network-routed distances and charging provision into a trip-level feasibility-screening framework. In the reference scenario, the framework assesses approximately `r sprintf("%.0f", r2_metrics$baseline_volume/1e6)` million retained synthetic local car-person trips per day across Scotland. Demographic and range screening with purpose weighting retains `r r2_pct(r2_metrics$screened_pre_access_volume)`\% of baseline demand as potentially suitable before charging constraints are considered. Charging-related constraints account for `r r2_pct(r2_metrics$access_excluded_volume + r2_metrics$conditional_volume)`\% of baseline demand: `r r2_pct(r2_metrics$access_excluded_volume)`\% are excluded because the required charging access is unavailable, while a further `r r2_pct(r2_metrics$conditional_volume)`\% have the required access but are constrained by charging capacity. This leaves an access-qualified theoretical share of `r r2_pct(r2_metrics$potential_volume)`\% of baseline demand, with `r r2_pct(r2_metrics$immediate_volume)`\% meeting assumed average-day charging-capacity requirements. Across separate sensitivity tests, theoretical shares range from `r sprintf("%.1f", r2_envelope[1])`\% to `r sprintf("%.1f", r2_envelope[2])`\%, while capacity-sufficient shares range from `r sprintf("%.1f", min(r2_scenario_totals$immediate_pct))`\% to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(r2_scenario_totals$immediate_pct))`\%. Substitution rates vary across 12 trip purposes, with `r abstract_totals$top1_purpose` and `r abstract_totals$top2_purpose` achieving the highest substitution rates (`r sprintf("%.1f", abstract_totals$top1_rate)`% and `r sprintf("%.1f", abstract_totals$top2_rate)`%), while `r volume_purposes_abstract$purpose[1]` and `r volume_purposes_abstract$purpose[2]` generate the largest absolute volumes of replaceable trips. The results identify spatial and purpose-specific opportunities for frugal-EV deployment under the stated scenarios; they do not predict realised adoption.

The proposed analytical methodology is transferable to any region/country with census-level demographic data and origin-destination records, although the trip-purpose feasibility rankings and shares reported here are calibrated to Scotland and require recalibration before generalising to other contexts.

# Keywords {.unnumbered}

Frugal electric vehicle; Gravity model trip simulation; Census-based adoption propensity; Charging constraint decomposition, Trip-level feasibility screening

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Highlights {.unnumbered}

- Assesses frugal EVs as potentially suitable alternatives for routine car travel.

- Integrates census demographics, routed trips, and charging access into a unified framework.

- Reports four volume components: screened-suitable, capacity-constrained, access-excluded, and the screen/purpose residual.

- Reveals spatial and trip-purpose variation in substitution potential.

- Modular modelling code and documented inputs support reproduction and transfer.


{{< pagebreak >}}

# Introduction

Transport electrification is central to national decarbonisation targets, with governments worldwide committing to phase out internal combustion engine (ICE) sales within the coming decade [@IEA2023; @IEA2025]. In Scotland, where transport accounts for 29% of territorial emissions, the net-zero target for 2045 and the five-year carbon-budget framework motivate further fleet decarbonisation [@ScottishCarbonBudgets2026]. Premium EVs with ranges exceeding 300 miles and prices above £42,000, exceeding the UK median equivalised household disposable income of approximately £36,700, remain inaccessible to lower-income households, rural communities, and those without dedicated parking [@SMMT2023; @Hardman2018; @ONS2024income].

This motivates examination of "frugal EVs", short-range vehicles (80–120 km AER, focusing on 100 km) priced at £6,000–£15,000, placing them within the price range of entry-level second-hand ICE vehicles and accessible to households priced out of mainstream EVs [@ElectrifyingUrbanMobility2025]. Frugal EVs are not merely cheaper electric cars: their limited range and modest charging speed are deliberate design choices, and it is those very limits that make them inexpensive, light on battery materials, and energy-efficient per kilometre. European quadricycles and Chinese mini-EVs confirm affordable electrification is feasible [@Zhao2024; @Palmer2018TCO], yet spatially disaggregated evidence on routine travel viability remains scarce. Over 70% of UK trips fall under 8 km [@DfT2022], while analysis of Germany's 2017 national household travel survey estimated that up to 76% of personal motorised trips could be served by at least one of nine light electric vehicle (LEV) categories under trip and user suitability criteria, including linked round trips [@Gebhardt2023]. The Scottish analysis evaluates retained synthetic local car-person trips generated with a 40 km destination-search setting. Its range-feasibility share is conditional on that generated population and does not establish the share of all Scottish car travel within frugal-EV range. Whether such vehicles serve as practical alternatives depends on demographic propensity, trip characteristics, infrastructure accessibility, and range constraints. Identifying the contexts in which they do therefore requires an integrated assessment of all four.

Several vehicles already on sale illustrate this segment, with the indicative, rounded specifications summarised in @tbl-frugal-models. The ZEV-UP project's two-seater and four-seater frugal EV prototypes are pictured in @fig-zevup-prototypes.

| Renault Twizy | Quadricycle (2) | ~80--100 km | ~GBP 10,000 | Microcar |

Scotland offers a particularly valuable case study for this analysis. Its settlement geography combines dense urban cores in the Central Belt, where flatted housing stock limits home charging, with dispersed rural communities served by sparse public charging networks and long inter-settlement distances. This spatial heterogeneity spans some of the UK's most and least charging-accessible areas, offering a demanding setting in which to evaluate an affordability-focused EV framework. The resulting evidence on how binding constraints shift across settlement contexts is expected to generalise to other regions with similarly mixed geographies.

The substitution question becomes substantive only for the resource-light frugal class, whose deliberate constraints mean that trip suitability must be demonstrated rather than assumed. Four gaps constrain policy application. First, representativeness bias toward premium models and higher-income adopters leaves affordable short-range alternatives under-examined: most evidence on EV adoption determinants derives from early-adopter samples concentrated in higher-income groups, limiting applicability to the frugal EV target market [@Rezvani2015; @Berkeley2018; @Plotz2014]. Second, many feasibility assessments rely on straight-line (Euclidean) distance, which underestimates actual road-network travel: road distances typically exceed straight-line distance by around 20–40% (a circuity factor of roughly 1.3, and higher in rural and coastal networks) [@Ballou2002], a bias disproportionately consequential for short-range vehicles where feasibility margins are narrow; the present analysis instead routes every trip over the road network. Third, charging infrastructure is often treated as uniformly available or uniformly absent, neglecting spatial heterogeneity in network density, access distance, and local demand that determines whether public charging can substitute for home charging in specific localities [@Funke2019; @Hardman2018; @Neubauer2014]. Fourth, trip-purpose heterogeneity receives limited integration: commuting, shopping, education, and leisure trips differ in route predictability, charging opportunity, and time flexibility, implying distinct substitution potentials and infrastructure requirements that aggregate assessments obscure [@Gebhardt2023].

This study addresses these gaps through an integrated feasibility framework combining demographic adoption propensity, trip-purpose suitability, network-routed range evaluation, and spatially resolved charging infrastructure assessment, applied to Scotland's 46,359 Output Areas and seven Regional Transport Partnerships (RTPs). The seven RTPs and their full names are listed in @tbl-rtp-glossary, which also indicates the dominant settlement character and signature city of each.

| Abbreviation | Full name | Character | Signature City |
|---|--------|---|---|
| SPT | Strathclyde Partnership for Transport | Urban | Glasgow |
| SEStran | South East of Scotland Transport Partnership | Mixed | Edinburgh |
| Tactran | Tayside and Central Scotland Transport Partnership | Mixed | Dundee |
| Nestrans | North East of Scotland Transport Partnership | Mixed | Aberdeen |
| HITRANS | Highlands and Islands Transport Partnership | Rural-island | Inverness |
| SWestrans | South West of Scotland Transport Partnership | Rural | Dumfries |
| ZetTrans | Shetland Transport Partnership | Rural-island | Lerwick |

: Scotland's seven Regional Transport Partnerships (RTPs), with full names, dominant settlement character, and signature city. {#tbl-rtp-glossary}

 Two methodological contributions result. First, the framework integrates gravity-based origin-destination simulation, Open Source Routing Machine (OSRM) network routing [@luxen-vetter-2011], and multiplicative feasibility constraints into a sequential pipeline that evaluates each trip against demographic, purpose, range, and infrastructure conditions, enabling identification of binding constraints at trip level rather than through regional averages. Second, a four-component volume decomposition reports screened-suitable, capacity-constrained, access-excluded, and the screen/purpose residual, providing an accounting framework that distinguishes where targeted charging deployment could help make adoption feasible from where structural barriers persist. Two empirical contributions emerge from the Scotland application. Third, purpose-disaggregated estimates across 12 trip types reveal roughly twofold variation in substitution rates, informing differentiated infrastructure investment strategies. Fourth, separate adoption-propensity (AP) band, distance-decay and purpose-weight scenarios quantify how the screening results depend on selected assumptions. Comparisons with battery electric vehicle (BEV) data assess component-level associations and do not independently validate substitution. Together, these contributions constitute a feasibility-screening framework that integrates demographic characteristics, trip purpose, network-routed vehicle range, and charging infrastructure conditions within a unified trip-level analytical pipeline. The volume components distinguish capacity-qualified substitution potential from public-capacity deficits and remaining baseline demand. Importantly, its purpose is to identify modelled trip-level feasibility under a defined set of assumptions rather than to predict actual adoption behaviour or vehicle replacement decisions.

The analysis estimates scenario-based suitability for frugal EVs among retained synthetic local car-person trips in Scotland, separating range-and-charging suitability from the effects of demographic screening and purpose weighting. Three sub-questions address this objective:

**RQ1:** Where and for whom do short-range EVs represent a feasible substitute for conventional car trips under current and near-term enhanced infrastructure conditions, and how can policy maximise substitution potential while ensuring equitable access?

**RQ2:** Which trip purposes offer highest substitution potential, and how do purpose-specific constraints inform infrastructure priorities?

**RQ3:** Where do charging infrastructure gaps most constrain feasible frugal EV substitution, and which deployment types align with regional trip patterns?

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. @sec-literature-review reviews the relevant literature and conceptual framing. @sec-framework presents the data, feasibility logic and analytical workflow. @sec-findings reports the Scottish application and its policy implications. @sec-limitations discusses methodological limitations, and @sec-conclusions draws conclusions.

# Literature Review {#sec-literature-review}

## Demographic and Geographic Determinants of EV Adoption

A substantial body of research has examined the socioeconomic and geographic determinants of EV adoption, consistently identifying income, education, housing tenure, parking access, and fleet composition as primary predictors [@Plotz2014; @Rezvani2015; @Hardman2018; @Chen2020; @Yiu2025BEVEngland]. Income and social grade are among the strongest documented predictors. In a spatial analysis of Hawaiian ZIP codes, Wee et al. [-@Wee2020] found that each $10,000 increase in median household income correlated with approximately 8% higher registered EV counts, and that areas with 1,000 additional degree-educated residents showed 19% higher EV registrations, suggesting education reflects information access and technology familiarity beyond income effects; in Massachusetts, Gehrke and Reardon [-@Gehrke2021] identified an interaction between single-family residence and the census-tract share of high-income households, with the number of public charging sites included as a separate predictor. UK research corroborates this pattern: higher purchase intention is observed among degree holders and multi-car households, indicating that affordability and practical need interact with attitudinal and informational factors [@Xu2023; @Yiu2025BEVEngland]. Housing imposes systematic barriers: 33% of UK households lack off-street parking, rising above 40% in dense urban areas, and most EV charging occurs at home where available, substantially disadvantaging lower-income households and renters [@ONS2021; @CMA2021; @Hardman2018; @AxsenKurani2012]. These findings collectively point to income, education, housing type, and parking access as the observable small-area indicators with the strongest empirical grounding and the greatest demonstrated influence on EV adoption outcomes.

Household fleet composition mediates range limitations. Multi-car households specialise vehicles by task, allocating short-range EVs to routine trips while retaining conventional vehicles for long journeys [@Davis2023]. Fleet flexibility absorbs range-anxiety and charging barriers that constrain single-car households. In an analysis of the US National Household Travel Survey, 89% of EV owners possessed a conventional vehicle [@Davis2023].

Price sensitivity constrains adoption among lower-income demographics. European consumers report median willingness-to-pay of €20,000 for BEVs versus €15,000 for conventional vehicles, whilst average EV prices exceed €45,000 [@EAFO2023]. Total cost of ownership analysis across UK, US, and Japanese markets finds that cost competitiveness depends strongly on purchase price and usage patterns, reinforcing the affordability case for lower-cost vehicle segments [@Palmer2018TCO; @LohNoland2024UsedEV].

## Trip-Purpose Heterogeneity and Substitution Potential

Travel behaviour reveals substantial heterogeneity in trip-purpose suitability for short-range EVs, with 12 categories varying in regularity, distance predictability, and charging compatibility [@NTS2022]. Commuting ranks among strongest candidates through fixed routes and overnight charging [@DfT2022], while shopping and personal business suit short-range vehicles through frequent local patterns.
Educational and escort trips align with predictable schedules, while business travel presents mixed suitability: urban visits fit short-range capabilities, multi-site itineraries remain challenging. Long-distance leisure travel, though infrequent, exerts outsized influence on vehicle choice as households purchase to accommodate maximum occasional need [@Turrentine2007; @Skippon2011UKAttitudes].

The proportion of trips falling within short-range EV capability depends substantially on this purpose composition. Gebhardt et al. [-@Gebhardt2023] reported somewhat higher theoretical substitution potential for commuting/work and private errands than for other purposes, relating this pattern to trip length and occupancy. Plötz et al. [-@Plotz2014] similarly identified commuting regularity and predictable daily driving patterns as characteristics of likely early EV adopters, suggesting that trip-purpose composition predicts adoption potential more reliably than aggregate distance alone. Charging behaviour research corroborates this: Franke and Krems [-@Franke2013] found that EV users with predictable trip routines developed more consistent and efficient charging strategies, adapting usage to vehicle capability in ways that irregular-travel users did not.

Despite this evidence, most feasibility assessments evaluate EV suitability at the vehicle or household level, aggregating across all trip types [@DaramyWilliams2019UserExperience]. This aggregation obscures the distinct substitution potential of individual purposes: a household that would readily replace commuting and shopping trips with an EV may nonetheless retain a conventional vehicle for less predictable or longer journeys. Disaggregating by trip purpose reveals that feasibility varies not only across geographies and demographic groups, but according to the trip-purpose composition of household travel; a distinction with direct implications for how charging infrastructure investment can most effectively expand EV viability.

## Range Feasibility and Real-World Performance Constraints

Laboratory Advertised Equivalent Range (AER) values systematically overestimate real-world performance. Testing programmes across Europe and North America document shortfalls of 10–30% relative to manufacturer claims, with cold weather, hilly terrain, motorway driving, and battery degradation compounding losses [@Steinstraeter2021ColdRange; @Wager2016; @Melliger2018; @ADAC2023; @AAA2019; @NAF2024; @Geotab2024]. Real-world data from GPS-equipped fleets corroborate that most routine driving falls comfortably within short-range capability: in one large naturalistic study, mean daily driving distance was 72 km, with trips exceeding 160 km on only 6% of days [@Pearre2011; @PlotzGnannWietschel2013]. These findings indicate that range anxiety, whilst psychologically significant, often overstates the practical constraint on everyday travel. Collectively, these performance gaps establish the empirical basis for conservative effective-range assumptions in feasibility assessments of short-range EVs.

## Infrastructure Investment and Deployment Strategies

Charging infrastructure is among the most effective policy levers for expanding EV adoption beyond the home-charging-capable segment. Where home charging is available, most charging occurs at home; where it is unavailable, access to public infrastructure becomes a prerequisite for EV ownership [@Hardman2018; @Speidel2014; @Neaimeh2017]. Quasi-experimental evidence indicates that public charger deployment stimulates adoption: van Dijk et al. [-@MITCEEPR2022] found 22–46% increases in EV registrations two years after first charger installations across Norwegian municipalities, whilst US studies document comparable positive responses [@Li2017; @Springel2021], consistent with a role for infrastructure in enabling uptake; because these are observational designs rather than controlled experiments, residual confounding from unobserved local demand cannot be fully excluded. European evidence from Norway similarly identifies public charging station density as the strongest predictor of county-level EV market share [@Mersky2016Norway; @Sierzchula2014]. Spatial analysis of public charger coverage reveals that walking-access distance is the critical friction variable: user preference research indicates approximately 500 m as an acceptable walk to a public charge point, with access distances exceeding 1 km substantially reducing usage propensity [@Budnitz2024; @Potoglou2023].

Research on network planning further identifies spatial clustering of chargers in high-income urban areas as an equity concern, with rural and lower-income areas systematically under-served relative to EV ownership rates [@Funke2019; @Nicholas2020; @Hopkins2023]. Infrastructure distribution strategies, including workplace charging, destination charging at retail and leisure venues, and corridor infill for inter-urban routes, have distinct alignment with different trip-purpose categories, suggesting that feasibility assessments benefit from purpose-disaggregated analysis. Battery-swapping experiments have explored alternatives to fixed infrastructure, but practical limitations including battery weights of approximately 40 kg for short-range vehicles indicate conventional fixed charging remains the prerequisite for mainstream deployment [@ElectrifyingUrbanMobility2025].

## Conceptual Framing

The preceding review demonstrates that existing studies address the determinants of EV adoption, specifically demographic propensity, trip-purpose compatibility, charging access, and vehicle range, largely in isolation from one another [@DaramyWilliams2019UserExperience; @Melliger2018]. An individual study may quantify income effects on adoption propensity without modelling whether the trips made by those households fall within the vehicle's capability; another may assess range feasibility without accounting for whether chargers are accessible at origin or destination. This fragmentation limits policy utility, because technical operating conditions and demographic market assumptions affect different quantities: range, charging access and capacity determine whether trips are screened as feasible within the selected scenario, while the demographic gate selects the market population and purpose suitability continuously weights potential. An integrated framework that captures these constraint interactions, rather than applying each condition independently, can identify where targeted interventions could help enable adoption and where the selected market or range screens are not met. The contribution of this study is therefore an integrated feasibility-screening pipeline that separates demographic market screening from the technical conditions defining screened-suitable and charging-constrained substitution opportunities.

Practical suitability is thus conditioned by whichever constraint binds most tightly in a given context: in dense urban areas, limited home-charging access may prevent adoption even where trips are short and demographics are favourable; in rural areas, range or infrastructure gaps may bind even where home charging is available [@Melliger2018; @Pareschi2020]. A framework that combines these dimensions while separating demographic screening from technical constraints, evaluating each trip against demographic, purpose, range, and infrastructure conditions simultaneously, can decompose aggregate feasibility into the contribution of each barrier, distinguishing where targeted policy intervention could help make adoption feasible from where multiple constraints compound to prevent it regardless of any single investment.

Constraint-based formulations of this kind characterise the technically feasible choice set, but they do not by themselves predict behaviour. Households decide under bounded rationality rather than full optimisation [@simon1955behavioral], weigh the loss of a familiar vehicle more heavily than equivalent gains [@kahneman1979prospect], and act on habit and default rather than recalculating each trip [@thaler2008nudge], so an intention to adopt frequently fails to translate into purchase or sustained use. Feasibility screening characterises scenario potential under defined structural assumptions: high-propensity households are screened out by scenario design, purpose weights discount candidate trips, and en-route charging is omitted.

# Integrated Analytical Framework {#sec-framework}

The framework defines data inputs, formalises feasibility logic, and operationalises eight implementation stages.
The eight-stage workflow addresses this overarching objective through its three sub-questions. RQ1 (where and for whom) is operationalised through Stage 2 (adoption propensity), combining demographic readiness with home charging to identify the target market. RQ2 (trip purposes) is addressed through Stage 3 (purpose compatibility), weighting 12 trip types by regularity, predictability, and charging flexibility. RQ3 (infrastructure gaps) is tackled through Stage 4 (charging infrastructure analysis), evaluating spatial accessibility and capacity. Stages 5–8 integrate these into trip-level feasibility classification.

# Ensure inline references to scotland_totals work before Results section
if (!exists("scotland_totals")) {
    suppressWarnings({
        library(jsonlite)
    })
    regions <- c("HITRANS", "Nestrans", "SESTRAN", "SPT", "SWESTRANS", "Tactran", "ZetTrans")
    regional_data_pre <- list()
    for (region in regions) {
        fp <- opath(region, paste0(region, "_comprehensive_summary.json"))
        if (file.exists(fp)) {
            regional_data_pre[[region]] <- jsonlite::fromJSON(fp)
        }
    }
    scotland_totals <- list(
        total_baseline_trips = sum(vapply(regional_data_pre, function(x) as.numeric(x$conversion_potential$total_baseline_trips), numeric(1)), na.rm = TRUE),
        total_demographic_areas = sum(vapply(regional_data_pre, function(x) as.numeric(x$data_coverage$demographic_areas), numeric(1)), na.rm = TRUE),
        total_charging_locations = sum(vapply(regional_data_pre, function(x) as.numeric(x$data_coverage$charging_locations), numeric(1)), na.rm = TRUE)
    )
}

```{r}
#| label: precompute-propensity-hcf-stats
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# Compute adoption propensity and HCF statistics for inline references
suppressWarnings({
    library(sf)
    library(dplyr)
})

regions <- c(
    "HITRANS", "Nestrans", "SESTRAN", "SPT",
    "SWESTRANS", "Tactran", "ZetTrans"
)
frugal_ap_lower <- 0.3
frugal_ap_upper <- 0.8

r2_target_band <- function(ap) {
    stopifnot(is.numeric(ap), all(is.finite(ap)), all(ap >= 0 & ap <= 1))
    ap >= frugal_ap_lower & ap <= frugal_ap_upper
}

r2_validate_oa_scores <- function(data, score_cols, context) {
    required <- c("geo_code", score_cols)
    if (!all(required %in% names(data))) {
        stop(context, ": required OA identifiers or scores are absent")
    }
    ids <- as.character(data$geo_code)
    if (anyNA(ids) || any(!nzchar(trimws(ids))) || anyDuplicated(ids)) {
        stop(context, ": OA identifiers must be present and unique")
    }
    for (score in score_cols) {
        values <- data[[score]]
        if (!is.numeric(values) || any(!is.finite(values)) ||
            any(values < 0 | values > 1)) {
            stop(context, ": ", score, " must contain complete scores in [0,1]")
        }
    }
    invisible(TRUE)
}

# Keep one canonical, frozen OA inventory for all area-count summaries.
stopifnot(
    all(c("region", "total_areas", "target_areas") %in% names(r2_oa_counts)),
    !anyNA(r2_oa_counts$region), !anyDuplicated(r2_oa_counts$region),
    setequal(regions, r2_oa_counts$region),
    is.numeric(r2_oa_counts$total_areas), is.numeric(r2_oa_counts$target_areas),
    all(is.finite(r2_oa_counts$total_areas)), all(is.finite(r2_oa_counts$target_areas)),
    all(r2_oa_counts$total_areas > 0),
    all(r2_oa_counts$total_areas == floor(r2_oa_counts$total_areas)),
    all(r2_oa_counts$target_areas == floor(r2_oa_counts$target_areas)),
    all(r2_oa_counts$target_areas >= 0),
    all(r2_oa_counts$target_areas <= r2_oa_counts$total_areas)
)
canonical_oa_by_region <- setNames(lapply(regions, function(region) {
    gpkg_path <- opath(region, "adoption_propensity_categorized.gpkg")
    stopifnot(file.exists(gpkg_path))
    region_data <- st_read(gpkg_path, quiet = TRUE)
    r2_validate_oa_scores(
        region_data,
        c("final_adoption_propensity", "home_charging_feasibility"), region
    )
    region_data <- region_data[, c(
        "geo_code", "final_adoption_propensity", "home_charging_feasibility"
    )]
    region_data$geo_code <- as.character(region_data$geo_code)
    expected <- r2_oa_counts[match(region, r2_oa_counts$region), ]
    stopifnot(
        nrow(region_data) == expected$total_areas,
        sum(r2_target_band(region_data$final_adoption_propensity)) == expected$target_areas
    )
    region_data$region <- region
    region_data
}), regions)
all_adoption_data <- bind_rows(lapply(canonical_oa_by_region, st_drop_geometry))
stopifnot(
    !anyDuplicated(all_adoption_data$geo_code),
    nrow(all_adoption_data) == sum(r2_oa_counts$total_areas)
)
total_oas <- nrow(all_adoption_data)

# The high-propensity group is strictly above the inclusive target band.
high_prop <- all_adoption_data %>%
    filter(final_adoption_propensity > frugal_ap_upper)
stopifnot(nrow(high_prop) > 0)
high_prop_hcf_pct <- 100 * sum(high_prop$home_charging_feasibility >= 0.5) / nrow(high_prop)

target_band <- all_adoption_data %>%
    filter(r2_target_band(final_adoption_propensity))
target_band_count <- nrow(target_band)
stopifnot(target_band_count > 0, target_band_count == sum(r2_oa_counts$target_areas))
target_band_pct <- 100 * target_band_count / total_oas
target_hcf_pct <- 100 * sum(target_band$home_charging_feasibility >= 0.5) / target_band_count

# Band-edge empirical evidence, read here (ahead of the band-rationale paragraph
# below, which references upper_changepoint and lower_floor_share inline) so the
# variables exist in document order. Precomputed by
# paper/scripts/band_edge_evidence.py; also re-read in the validation section.
band_ev <- read.csv("../results/validation/band_edge_evidence_summary.csv",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
upper_changepoint <- band_ev$value[band_ev$metric == "upper_changepoint_1bp"]
lower_floor_share <- band_ev$value[band_ev$metric == "lower_band_bev_share_pct"]
```

## Data Inputs

The analysis integrates four primary datasets for Scotland: (1) demographic indicators from Scotland's Census 2022 [@scotlandcensus2022][^data-demographic], covering 46,359 Output Areas and capturing accommodation type, age-sex structure, social grade, car availability, economic activity, education, household composition, and density; (2) synthetic origin-destination travel matrices generated from zone populations, a pre-COVID baseline of 2.61 trips per person per day, and Scottish Household Survey purpose shares[^data-od], encompassing `r sprintf("%.0f", r2_metrics$baseline_volume/1e6)` million retained synthetic local car-person trips per day across 12 purposes and seven RTPs, spatially disaggregated using gravity-based interaction and jittering methods [@lovelace2022jittering]; travel survey data provide a validated basis for EV feasibility modelling, with simulated charging profiles derived from household travel surveys shown to correspond closely with empirical charging data [@Pareschi2020]; (3) network routing via OSRM with OpenStreetMap[^data-routing], providing realistic driving distances that typically exceed Euclidean by 20–40%; and (4) `r format(scotland_totals$total_charging_locations, big.mark=",")` public charging locations from OpenChargeMap[^data-charging].

[^data-od]: Source datasets: National Travel Survey trip-rate statistics and Scottish Household Survey travel data [@NTS2020; @SHS2019]. The OD matrices are synthetic rather than directly observed: trip productions are generated by applying the latest stable pre-COVID baseline of 2.61 trips per person per day to zone populations and allocating those trips across the twelve modelled purposes using Scottish Household Survey shares. The twelve purposes are the fourteen Scottish Household Survey travel-diary purposes (table TD3) without separate Go home and Go for a walk classes. Preprocessing redistributes the Go home share across the other survey purposes before excluding Go for a walk. Retained demand is measured in one-way car-person trips. Symmetric round-trip evaluation is a range-screening assumption, not an instruction to double the OD volumes or generate additional return records. Destinations are then distributed through the spatial interaction model described in [Appendix A.1](#sec-od-disaggregation-appendix). Trip production retains the generator's 2011 residential population control, whereas demographic scoring uses the 2022 Census. This mixed-vintage specification and the generation/filtering exclusions distinguish the modelled denominator from a contemporary count of all Scottish car journeys. Census data portal: <https://www.scotlandscensus.gov.uk/>. Flows are recorded between zone centroids; before routing, each zone-to-zone flow is spatially disaggregated by the jittering method of @lovelace2022jittering, splitting it into multiple origin-destination point pairs in proportion to trip counts so that routing reflects a realistic diversity of departure and arrival locations rather than a single centroid-to-centroid path.
[^data-routing]: Routing stack: Open Source Routing Machine (OSRM) with OpenStreetMap road network data [@luxen-vetter-2011]. OSRM project: <https://project-osrm.org/>; OpenStreetMap: <https://www.openstreetmap.org/>. Routing applies the OSRM driving profile. As an independent check, OSRM driving distances were compared with Google Routing API distances on a sample of SESTRAN commute routes whose request points could be matched within 300 m at both endpoints (14 routes): the two sources agree closely (Pearson correlation 0.88; median absolute difference 5.8 per cent; median ratio of OSRM to Google distance 0.97).
[^data-demographic]: Small-area demographic indicators are taken from Scotland's Census 2022 Output Area tables, released March 2025 by National Records of Scotland [@scotlandcensus2022]. Data portal: <https://www.scotlandscensus.gov.uk/>.
[^data-charging]: Public charging locations extracted from OpenChargeMap (August 2025), with ChargePlace Scotland statistics (~2,900 charge points) used for contextual benchmarking [@ChargePlace2024; @Nicholas2020]. OpenChargeMap data/API: <https://openchargemap.org/site/develop/api>.
[^data-mot]: Component and threshold-study data: electric-coded vehicles observed in Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) MOT records, aggregated to postcode areas. Grid 3 includes all test outcomes and first-use years; the threshold and price-segment studies retain passing tests and the stated first-use cohorts (Appendix B.2). These records are not a complete series of new registrations. DVSA MOT dataset: <https://open.data.dvsa.gov.uk/mot/index.html>.
[^data-hpi]: Control/contextual dataset: Registers of Scotland property transaction statistics aggregated from Data Zones to postcode area level through 2022 (labelled HPI in repository calibration workflows). Registers of Scotland property market data: <https://www.ros.gov.uk/data-and-statistics/property-market-statistics>.

## Core Feasibility Logic

The framework introduces a hierarchical screening rule within an eight-stage workflow, separating pre-access mobility suitability from infrastructure qualification. A trip satisfies the pre-access mobility and demographic screen ($S_{ij}=1$) only when: (1) the origin Output Area falls within the frugal-EV target market by adoption propensity; and (2) the network-routed trip distance does not exceed effective range. Access-qualified eligibility ($R_{ij}=1$) additionally requires that: (3) the applicable charging condition is met at origin and, for medium-length trips, at destination. Baseline trip demand meeting these criteria is then scaled by purpose-suitability weights to determine substitution volumes. This constraint-based approach follows the precedent of vehicle substitution screening [@Tamor2013; @Neubauer2014], where the relevant policy question is which trips meet the specified scenario-dependent screening conditions, rather than the probability that households will actually adopt or use a frugal EV. The pre-access screen and access-qualified indicator are defined in @eq-feasibility-indicator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{ij}
  &{}= \underbrace{\mathbf{1}\{AP_i^{\min} \leq AP_i \leq AP_i^{\max}\}}_{\text{condition (1): demographic target band}}
  \cdot
  \underbrace{\mathbf{1}\{d_{ij}\leq R_{\text{eff}}\}}_{\text{condition (2): effective range limit}}
\\[0.8em]
R_{ij}
  &= S_{ij}
  \cdot
  \underbrace{\mathbf{1}\{C_{ij} = 1\}}_{\text{condition (3): charging access condition}}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-feasibility-indicator}

$$
R_{eff} = R_{AER} \cdot \beta_{buffer}
$$ {#eq-effective-range}

$$
C_{ij} = \begin{cases}
H_i \lor \Pi_i & \text{if } d_{ij} \leq R_{\text{eff}}/2 \text{ (OR logic)} \\
(H_i \lor \Pi_i) \land \Pi_j & \text{if } R_{\text{eff}}/2 < d_{ij} \leq R_{\text{eff}} \text{ (AND logic)} \\
0 & \text{if } d_{ij} > R_{\text{eff}}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-charging-condition}

where $S_{ij} \in \{0,1\}$ is the pre-access mobility suitability indicator, and $R_{ij} \in \{0,1\}$ is the access-qualified eligibility indicator for a trip from origin $i$ to destination $j$, $AP_i$ is adoption propensity at origin with target range $AP_i^{\min}$ to $AP_i^{\max}$; $d_{ij}$ is network-routed distance; $R_{eff}$ is effective range from nominal $R_{AER}$ and buffer $\beta_{buffer}$; $C_{ij}$ is charging condition; $H_i$ indicates home charging feasibility; and $\Pi_i,\Pi_j$ indicate public charging accessibility at origin and destination respectively. Short trips ($d_{ij} \leq R_{\text{eff}}/2$) require charging at origin only, satisfied by either home or nearby public charging ($H_i \lor \Pi_i$). Medium trips ($R_{\text{eff}}/2 < d_{ij} \leq R_{\text{eff}}$) require home or nearby public charging at origin, together with destination charging ($(H_i \lor \Pi_i) \land \Pi_j$), reflecting that a single charge is insufficient for the round trip and en-route charging is not assumed. Trips exceeding $R_{\text{eff}}$ fall outside the screened scenario regardless of charging availability. Trips meeting demographic and range criteria ($S_{ij}=1$) but lacking charging access ($C_{ij}=0$) are classified as access-excluded.

*Modelling simplification:* Each OD pair is evaluated as a symmetric round trip for range screening, while demand remains measured in one-way car-person trips. Three charging modes are included in the baseline model: (a) home charging at origin, represented by $H_i = \mathbf{1}\{HCF_i \geq 0.5\}$; (b) public charging at origin, represented by $\Pi_i$, indicating a charger within 0.5 km of the origin OA centroid; and (c) public charging at destination, represented by $\Pi_j$, using the same 0.5 km threshold. Public-capacity checks apply at origin when $H_i=0$ and at destination for all medium-distance trips (40--80 km). Home charging is considered possible when the HCF threshold is met, without a separate installed-capacity assessment. En-route charging and battery swapping are excluded from the baseline model.
The adoption-propensity band $AP_i^{\min}=0.30$ to $AP_i^{\max}=0.80$ in @eq-feasibility-indicator defines the reference frugal-EV segment using demographic composition, car ownership and charging conditions. Below 0.30, `r sprintf("%.1f", ap_profiles$no_car_pct[1])`\% of households have no car or van, compared with `r sprintf("%.1f", ap_profiles$no_car_pct[2])`\% within the band, while mean home-charging scores are `r sprintf("%.3f", ap_profiles$home_charging_mean[1])` and `r sprintf("%.3f", ap_profiles$home_charging_mean[2])`, respectively. The lower edge therefore distinguishes the lowest-readiness group from the broader car-using population targeted by the scenario. Local composition models locate a common transition near 0.29, although the transition involves different directions of change in social grade, housing and car ownership.
The upper edge separates the most materially advantaged profiles: above 0.80, `r sprintf("%.1f", ap_profiles$multi_car_pct[3])`\% of households have at least two cars or vans, and `r sprintf("%.1f", ap_profiles$abc1_pct[3])`\% of the social-grade population is ABC1. At Data-Zone scale, the median of local median house prices rises from GBP `r format(round(ap_dz_profiles$median_of_dz_median_price[2]), big.mark=",")` within the band to GBP `r format(round(ap_dz_profiles$median_of_dz_median_price[3]), big.mark=",")` above it. The fitted change in private-BEV uptake occurs at AP = `r sprintf("%.3f", ap_stat("bev_rate", "estimated_one", "lower"))`, close to the reference upper edge. These patterns motivate a focus on the intermediate, affordability-oriented segment rather than the highest-readiness conventional-BEV market.
The price-segmented MOT comparisons in @sec-adoption-results describe the corresponding lower-price and premium vehicle patterns. A threshold-specific study in [Appendix B.7](#sec-ap-threshold-study) examines local and global demographic changes, house-price gradients and household-normalised MOT outcomes. The cut-offs summarise these transitions as reference boundaries. The reference band did not improve household-normalised lower-price MOT prediction over house price alone. It is therefore retained as a scenario definition, not an independently validated frugal-EV market boundary. The sensitivity of the theoretical and capacity-sufficient substitution shares to alternative band boundaries is reported in @tbl-band-edge-headline. The paired results in @tbl-demographic-screen quantify their effect on trip substitution.




## Eight-Stage Workflow and Operationalisation

@fig-framework and @tbl-stage-map present the workflow, linking stages to governing equations; @tbl-notation defines principal symbols for operationalising the retained population of `r format(round(r2_metrics$rows), big.mark=",")` routed OD records across Scotland's seven RTPs. These are disaggregated routed records, not a count of distinct zone-to-zone pairs. Component diagnostics compare model scores with Scottish MOT electric-vehicle records from the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA)[^data-mot] and use house-sale statistics (labelled HPI in the component outputs)[^data-hpi] as covariates. Reference weights and multipliers are stated as modelling assumptions; Appendix B distinguishes these assumptions from component diagnostics and sensitivity analyses of substitution outcomes.



![Flowchart of the analytical framework](figures/framework.jpg){#fig-framework width=100%}

| Stage | Core Function | Key Equation(s) |
|-------|---------------|-----------------|
| Stage 1 | Integrate OD, demographic, and spatial data | @eq-gravity-model |
| Stage 2 | Compute adoption propensity | @eq-demographic-score, @eq-home-charging-feasibility, @eq-final-adoption |
| Stage 3 | Estimate purpose-level compatibility | @eq-trip-purpose-weight, @eq-trip-category |
| Stage 4 | Assess charging accessibility and capacity | @eq-home-charging-binary, @eq-public-charging-access, @eq-utilisation |
| Stage 5 | Evaluate range and charging feasibility | @eq-effective-range, @eq-charging-condition |
| Stage 6 | Estimate trip substitution under suitability rules | @eq-feasibility-indicator, @eq-trip-conversion, @eq-trip-classification |
| Stage 7 | Assign vehicle type | @eq-two-seater-score, @eq-four-seater-score, @eq-ev-type-assignment |
| Stage 8 | Aggregate system-level substitution potential | @eq-replacement-rate |
: Integrated stage map linking workflow components to key equations. {#tbl-stage-map}

| $j$ | Destination | - |

| $C_{ij}$ | Charging condition | {0,1} |
