: Principal notation used in the analytical framework. {#tbl-notation}

*Stage 1: Data Integration and Preprocessing*

This stage integrates OD flows, routing outputs, charging data, and census attributes at OA level.

**OD Disaggregation:** Zone-to-zone flows are transformed into point-to-point desire lines using a production-constrained gravity model [@Fotheringham1989]:

$$
T_{ij} = O_i \cdot \frac{A_j \cdot f(d_{ij}^{E})}{\sum_k A_k \cdot f(d_{ik}^{E})}
$$ {#eq-gravity-model}

where $T_{ij}$ is trips from origin $i$ to destination $j$, $O_i$ is origin production, $A_j$ is destination attractiveness, and $f(d_{ij}^{E})$ is distance-decay. $d_{ij}^{E}$ denotes pre-jitter straight-line geographic distance approximation in metres, distinct from the network-routed distance $d_{ij}$ in kilometres used for vehicle screening. For purpose $p$, $f(d_{ij}^{E})=\exp\left(\beta_p d_{ij}^{E}/1000\right)$, where $\beta_p<0$ is the coefficient in km$^{-1}$ supplied by the NTS-informed generation parameterisation. Division by 1,000 converts the gravity distance to kilometres. Weighted destination sampling and subsequent distance filtering are specified in Appendix A.1. The production-constrained specification preserves the modelled origin productions whilst estimating destination shares; the appropriate form when zone-level trip productions are known from census data but fine-grained destination totals are unavailable for all 12 purposes at Output Area resolution. A doubly-constrained model would require both origin and destination totals, which are not available at this level of spatial and purpose disaggregation [@Fotheringham1989; @Ortuzar2011]. Full implementation is in [Appendix A.1](#sec-od-disaggregation-appendix).

**Demographic Data Preprocessing:** Eight census domains (social grade, education, transport, housing, age, economic activity, household composition, density) are standardised and spatially joined at Output Area level [@scotlandcensus2022].


*Stage 2: Frugal EV Adoption Propensity Assessment*

Adoption propensity is estimated for each Output Area by combining demographic readiness, home charging feasibility, and geographic interactions. The demographic score uses reference weights (@tbl-sensitivity-calibration):

$$
S_{demo,i} = 0.45 \cdot SG_i + 0.25 \cdot ED_i + 0.20 \cdot CO_i + 0.10 \cdot HT_i
$$ {#eq-demographic-score}

where $SG_i$, $ED_i$, $CO_i$, and $HT_i$ are normalised component scores in $[0,1]$ ([Appendix A.2](#sec-demographic-scoring-appendix)). The reference specification assigns the largest weight (0.45) to social grade. Grid 1 examines eight demographic-component weighting schemes, including an equal-weight alternative, across six score caps and five thresholds. These diagnostics compare component-score aggregates with postcode-area MOT BEV counts (@tbl-sensitivity-calibration). Sensitivity of the theoretical and capacity-sufficient trip shares is assessed separately in Appendix B.1. Sub-component scoring equations are in [Appendix A.2](#sec-demographic-scoring-appendix).

Home charging feasibility (HCF) combines accommodation suitability and parking availability:

$$
HCF_i = w_a \cdot A_i + w_p \cdot P_i
$$ {#eq-home-charging-feasibility}

where $A_i$ is accommodation feasibility and $P_i$ is parking availability ([Appendix A.3](#sec-home-charging-feasibility-appendix)). Accommodation scores reflect off-street parking prevalence by dwelling type: detached and semi-detached houses score 0.92, flats score 0.22, and other types score 0.50 [@Nicholas2020]. Parking availability receives the dominant blend weight ($w_p = 0.80$) because UK evidence consistently identifies off-street parking access as the binding constraint on home charger installation, over and above dwelling type [@Hardman2021; @CMA2021]; full derivation is in [Appendix A.3](#sec-home-charging-feasibility-appendix).

The base score is then adjusted by interaction and geography multipliers:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{demo,i}' &= S_{demo,i} \cdot M_{IE,i}
  \cdot M_{MC,i} \cdot M_{AI,i},\\
S_{demo,i}'' &{}= \min\left(1,\max\left(0,S_{demo,i}'\cdot M_{\rho,i}\right)\right).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-interaction-effects}

where $M_{IE,i}$, $M_{{MC},i}$, $M_{AI,i}$, and $M_{\rho,i}$ capture income-education synergy, multi-car advantage, age-income interaction, and density effects respectively ([Appendix A.4](#sec-demographic-interactions-appendix)). The appendix uses the equivalent symbols $IE_i$, $MC_i$, $AI_i$ and $PD_i$ for these four multipliers. Bounding is applied after the interaction and geographic multipliers and before the final AP blend. The income-education interaction is specified through assumed multipliers: 1.60 for Output Areas where both social grade ($SG_i > 0.7$) and education ($ED_i > 0.7$) scores are high, and a compound penalty of 0.50 where both are low. The literature context and limits of this assumption are described in Appendix B.3. Density adjustments penalise remote areas (0.70 multiplier for population densities below 10 persons/km²) and apply a modest suburban premium (1.08 for 200–1,000 persons/km²), consistent with observed infrastructure access gradients [@CMA2021]; full piecewise specifications enabling replication are in [Appendix A.4](#sec-demographic-interactions-appendix).

Adoption Propensity (AP) Score is defined as:
$$
AP_i = w_{demo} \cdot S_{demo,i}'' + w_{charge} \cdot HCF_i
$$ {#eq-final-adoption}

where the final adoption propensity combines adjusted demographic score and home-charging feasibility. The reference specification assigns 70% weight to demographic readiness ($w_{demo}=0.70$) and 30% to home-charging feasibility ($w_{charge}=0.30$). This blend is a modelling assumption that gives demographic readiness greater influence while retaining a contribution from residential charging feasibility. Grid 1 varies the four demographic-component weights and does not estimate the demographic--home-charging blend.


*Stage 3: Trip Purpose Compatibility Assessment*

Purpose-specific compatibility is estimated using regularity, predictability, and charging flexibility [@NTS2022; @DfT2022; @Franke2013]. Each purpose is represented by behavioural parameters informed by NTS/SHS evidence and expert judgement; @tbl-trip-purpose-inputs summarises scoring values. These are expert-assigned ordinal ratings calibrated against observed trip characteristics (frequency, dwell-time, scheduling) from the DfT National Travel Survey for England [@NTS2022; @DfT2022] and Scottish Household Survey shares [@SHS2019]. Sensitivity is addressed through the trip-purpose weighting grid, which varies the aggregation weights, and a dedicated robustness analysis that additionally perturbs the ordinal ratings themselves ([Appendix B](#app-sensitivity-calibration)).

| Trip Purpose | Regularity ($R_p$) | Predictability ($T_p$) | Dwell Flexibility ($D_p$) | Temporal Sensitivity ($S_p$) |
|-------------------------------|-------------------|----------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Commuting | 0.950 | 0.900 | 0.9 | 0.9 |
| Education | 0.900 | 0.850 | 0.9 | 0.9 |
| Shopping | 0.650 | 0.700 | 0.9 | 0.5 |
| Health visits | 0.600 | 0.800 | 0.9 | 0.9 |
| Escort | 0.700 | 0.800 | 0.1 | 0.7 |
| Other personal business | 0.400 | 0.500 | 0.5 | 0.7 |
| Business | 0.400 | 0.500 | 0.5 | 0.9 |
| Eating/drinking | 0.400 | 0.500 | 0.3 | 0.3 |
| Sport/entertainment | 0.500 | 0.600 | 0.3 | 0.5 |
| Visiting friends/relatives | 0.300 | 0.400 | 0.7 | 0.1 |
| Other journey | 0.300 | 0.400 | 0.3 | 0.1 |
| Holiday/day-trip | 0.100 | 0.300 | 0.7 | 0.1 |
: Trip purpose input parameters for the twelve modelled trip purposes. Parameters informed by the DfT National Travel Survey for England [@NTS2022; @DfT2022] and Scottish Household Survey travel data [@SHS2019]. {#tbl-trip-purpose-inputs}


The Trip Purpose suitability weight is calculated as:

$$
W^{(p)} = w_R \cdot R_p + w_T \cdot T_p + w_{CF} \cdot CF_p
$$ {#eq-trip-purpose-weight}

where $R_p$ is regularity, $T_p$ is predictability, $CF_p$ is charging flexibility (calculated from dwell flexibility, temporal sensitivity, infrastructure access, and home charging feasibility; see @eq-charging-flexibility-app), and weights $w_R = 0.35$, $w_T = 0.35$, and $w_{CF} = 0.30$ ([Appendix A.5](#sec-trip-purpose-charging-flexibility-appendix)). The charging flexibility component $CF_p$ is a weighted composite of four sub-components: dwell-time flexibility ($D_p$) receives the largest sub-weight ($w_{dwell} = 0.40$) because longer parking durations most directly enable opportunistic slow charging of frugal EVs; temporal sensitivity contributes at $w_{timing} = 0.30$, with less time-constrained trips offering more charging windows; destination infrastructure availability and home charging feasibility contribute the remainder ($w_{dest} = 0.20$, $w_{home} = 0.10$) [@Hardman2018; @Franke2013]. Full derivation is in [Appendix A.5](#sec-trip-purpose-charging-flexibility-appendix).

Trip purposes are grouped into three classes:

$$
Category^{(p)} = \begin{cases}
\text{High} & \text{if } W^{(p)} \geq 0.80 \\
\text{Medium} & \text{if } 0.50 \leq W^{(p)} < 0.80 \\
\text{Low} & \text{if } W^{(p)} < 0.50
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-trip-category}

where displayed cutoffs (0.50, 0.80) are rounded from calibrated thresholds reported in [Appendix B.4](#sec-trip-purpose-cutoff-calibration-appendix).

*Modelling simplification:* Trips are analysed independently rather than as chained tours. Trip chaining, where multiple stops are made on a single outing, can extend total travel distance beyond what any individual leg suggests; independent-trip screening may therefore overstate tour-level suitability. The chaining sensitivity analysis ([Appendix B.6](#sec-chaining-sensitivity)) applies a conditional loss only to access-qualified, home-chargeable trips of at most 40 km.


*Stage 4: Charging Infrastructure Analysis*

This stage evaluates charging access and public capacity at the required trip endpoints. Access determines eligibility, while shared public capacity determines whether eligible demand can be served under the reference operating assumptions.

Home charging availability is binarised as:

$$
H_i = \mathbf{1}\{HCF_i \geq \tau_{HCF}\}
$$ {#eq-home-charging-binary}

where $H_i \in \{0,1\}$ and $\tau_{HCF}=0.5$ ([Appendices A.5-A.6](#sec-trip-purpose-charging-flexibility-appendix)).

Public charging accessibility is represented as:

$$
\Pi_i = \mathbf{1}\{d_{nearest,i} \leq d_{max}\}
$$ {#eq-public-charging-access}

where $\Pi_i \in \{0,1\}$ and $d_{max}=0.5$ km ([Appendix A.6](#sec-charging-infrastructure-analysis-appendix)). The 0.5 km cut-off reflects evidence on user walk-access tolerance to charging and parking facilities [@Budnitz2024; @Potoglou2023]; it is a deliberately national-scale simplification, applying one straight-line distance uniformly across urban and rural Output Areas rather than modelling local pedestrian networks or kerbside availability.

To translate trip distance into charger-time demand, energy use and charging duration are:

$$
E_{ij} = d_{ij} \cdot \eta_{type}, \quad t_{ij} = \frac{E_{ij}}{P_{charge}}
$$ {#eq-energy-consumption}

where $\eta_{type}$ is fixed at 0.065 kWh/km for all flows in the headline capacity calculation and $P_{charge}$ is charger power ([Appendix A.6](#sec-charging-infrastructure-analysis-appendix)). The representative charger power $P_{charge} = 7$ kW corresponds to a standard UK Type 2 AC charger, which accounts for the majority of the public charging network and is appropriate for the slow-charging profile of frugal EVs. Although prototype specifications distinguish between 2-seater (7 kWh battery, 0.060 kWh/km) and 4-seater (11 kWh battery, 0.065 kWh/km) archetypes (@tbl-energy-params), these parameters serve as illustrative archetype benchmarks rather than distinct operational inputs in the network model: the headline operational calculations apply uniform parameters ($0.065$ kWh/km, $7$ kW charger power, and $80$ km effective range) across all flows, adopting the higher consumption rate as a conservative capacity assumption.

*Modelling simplification:* Charging-time calculations use this representative power rating rather than dynamic, time-varying power delivery. Real-world charging rates vary with battery state of charge, temperature, and charger condition; the representative value provides a consistent comparison basis but does not capture peak-demand degradation effects.

Public charging demand is pooled at physical location $\ell$. Let $a(i)$ and $a(j)$ identify the nearest site within 0.5 km of the origin OA centroid and generated destination, respectively. Each site's reported point count contributes once to the capacity shared by both endpoint roles. Charger assignment and capacity assessment are performed separately within each RTP using stations located within that RTP. Purpose-specific occupancy $o_p$ converts car-person flows to vehicle-equivalent demand. The baseline transfers England's 2019 NTS0905 car/van occupancy means to the Scottish flows [@DfTNTS0905]. Required charger-time is:

$$
D_\ell = \sum_{i,j,p}\frac{f_{ij}^{(p)}W^{(p)}R_{ij}}{o_p}\,t_{ij}
\left[s^O_{ij}\mathbf{1}\{a(i)=\ell\}+s^D_{ij}\mathbf{1}\{a(j)=\ell\}\right].
$$ {#eq-demand-definition}

The charging-energy shares $(s^O_{ij},s^D_{ij})$ are $(0,0)$ for home-chargeable short trips, $(1,0)$ for short trips relying on public charging, and $(0,1)$ for home-chargeable medium trips. Medium trips relying on public charging at both ends use $(0.5,0.5)$ in the reference allocation. This allocation counts the modelled one-way energy once while loading both required sites.

Capacity utilisation is defined as required charger-hours divided by available charger-hours:

$$
u_\ell = \frac{D_\ell}{16n_\ell(1-U_\ell^{bg})},\qquad
Cap_k=\mathbf{1}\{a(k)\text{ exists},\ n_{a(k)}>0,\ u_{a(k)}\leq1\},\quad k\in\{i,j\}.
$$ {#eq-utilisation}

where $n_\ell$ is the reported point count and $U_\ell^{bg}$ reserves capacity for background use. A missing location, non-positive point count or overload gives $Cap_k=0$. An unreported point count establishes access but supplies zero quantified capacity in the reference scenario. The reference scenario assumes a 16-hour operating day and background utilisation with base rate 0.45 and a size-dependent hub adjustment. [Appendix A.6](#sec-charging-infrastructure-analysis-appendix) gives the calculation. At an overloaded site, all dependent eligible trips are classified as capacity-constrained. The model does not allocate partial service or reroute them to alternative sites. The capacity-sufficient volume is therefore a screening classification, not maximum network throughput. Adding access may also increase shared-site demand, so access-excluded and capacity-constrained volumes cannot be treated as independent forecasts of gains from infrastructure investment. The paired scenarios in @tbl-demographic-screen recompute shared station demand whenever the AP screen or purpose weighting changes.

*Modelling simplification:* The capacity condition $Cap_k$ in @eq-utilisation is assessed against average daily charger demand rather than a temporal or peak-queuing model. Utilisation $u_\ell$ compares required charger-hours over a full operating day with available charger-hours, so it cannot detect peak-hour demand concentrations that create queuing at high-utilisation sites; this average-based check may therefore overstate charging availability at commuter-heavy destinations during morning or evening peaks. This is a national-scale simplification adopted because temporally resolved arrival profiles are not available for all destinations across Scotland's seven RTPs.


*Stage 5: Range Feasibility Assessment*

Range feasibility tests each network-routed OD distance against the conservative effective-range limit derived in Core Feasibility Logic. The 20% buffer ($\beta_{buffer} = 0.8$) applied to the 100 km nominal AER accommodates real-world performance degradation from cold Scottish weather conditions, terrain variation, and battery ageing [@Wager2016; @AAA2019]. The resulting 80 km effective range defines a graduated constraint: trips of 40 km or less require only origin charging; trips between 40 and 80 km require both origin and destination charging; trips exceeding 80 km are classified as range-infeasible regardless of charging availability. This graduated structure distinguishes the framework from simpler binary range checks that apply a single distance threshold, and directly motivates the OR/AND charging logic in @eq-charging-condition. Effective range $R_{eff}$ and charging condition $C_{ij}$ are formally defined in @eq-effective-range and @eq-charging-condition.


*Stage 6: Trip Substitution Estimation*

Stage 6 estimates purpose-weighted substitution volumes from baseline OD demand and the eligibility indicator in @eq-feasibility-indicator:

$$
N_{ij}^{(p)} = f_{ij}^{(p)} \cdot R_{ij} \cdot W^{(p)}
$$ {#eq-trip-conversion}

where $f_{ij}^{(p)}$ is baseline daily demand, $R_{ij}$ is the eligibility indicator in @eq-feasibility-indicator, and $W^{(p)}\in[0,1]$ is the purpose-suitability weight defined in @eq-trip-purpose-weight.

Eligibility indicators ($S_{ij}, R_{ij}$) under @eq-feasibility-indicator and charging capacity determine trip classification. Capacity qualification is $B_{ij}=(H_i\lor Cap_i)\land(\mathbf{1}\{d_{ij}\leq R_{\mathrm{eff}}/2\}\lor Cap_j)$. Origin public capacity is required only when $H_i=0$, while destination capacity is additionally required for 40--80 km trips. The trip-level classification and the daily volume components obtained from @eq-trip-conversion are:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{Class}_{ij} = \begin{cases}
\text{screened-suitable} & \text{if } R_{ij}=1 \land B_{ij}=1,\\
\text{capacity-constrained} & \text{if } R_{ij}=1 \land B_{ij}=0,\\
\text{access-excluded} & \text{if } S_{ij}=1 \land C_{ij}=0,\\
\text{outside demographic/range screen} & \text{if } S_{ij}=0,
\end{cases}
\\[1em]
\begin{aligned}
V_{\mathrm{screened}}
  &{}= \sum_{i,j,p} N_{ij}^{(p)} B_{ij},\\
V_{\mathrm{cap\_constrained}}
  &{}= \sum_{i,j,p} N_{ij}^{(p)}(1-B_{ij}),\\
V_{\mathrm{access\_excluded}}
  &{}= \sum_{i,j,p} f_{ij}^{(p)} S_{ij} (1-C_{ij}) W^{(p)},\\
V_{\mathrm{remaining}}
  &{}= \sum_{i,j,p} f_{ij}^{(p)} - (V_{\mathrm{screened}} + V_{\mathrm{cap\_constrained}} + V_{\mathrm{access\_excluded}}).
\end{aligned}
\end{gathered}
$$ {#eq-trip-classification}

The screened-suitable ($V_{\mathrm{screened}}$) and capacity-constrained ($V_{\mathrm{cap\_constrained}}$) volumes aggregate purpose-weighted demand in their respective classes and together equal the theoretical substitution volume ($N = \sum_{i,j,p} N_{ij}^{(p)}$). Access-excluded demand ($V_{\mathrm{access\_excluded}}$) captures trips satisfying the demographic and range screens ($S_{ij}=1$) that lack required home or local public charging access ($C_{ij}=0$). Combined, charging-related constraints ($V_{\mathrm{access\_excluded}} + V_{\mathrm{cap\_constrained}}$) account for `r r2_pct(r2_metrics$access_excluded_volume + r2_metrics$conditional_volume)`\% of baseline travel, identifying infrastructure interventions ranging from network coverage expansion to capacity augmentation. Note that while $\mathrm{Class}_{ij}$ partitions individual journeys into discrete eligibility states, the volume components scale eligible demand by the continuous purpose suitability weight $W^{(p)} \in [0,1]$. Consequently, the screen and purpose residual ($V_{\mathrm{remaining}}$) accounts for both journeys outside the demographic and range screens ($S_{ij}=0$) and the purpose-weight reduction $(1 - W^{(p)})$ across screened journeys ($S_{ij}=1$). The volume components sum to baseline daily car-person-trip demand and use that common denominator for their reported shares. Capacity qualification represents average-day provision under the modelled operating conditions.


*Stage 7: EV Type Selection*

Vehicle type (2-seater vs 4-seater) is assigned using household-demographic signals [@Oakil2014]. Census-derived household composition data provide the demographic proxy: small households and older age profiles favour 2-seater assignment, whilst households with children require 4-seater capacity. Regional vehicle-type proportions are fixed allocation assumptions in the reported scenarios.

Assignment scores use household size, age adjustment, and children presence:

$$
S_{2s,i} = w_{hs} \cdot HSF_i + w_{age} \cdot AAF_i {\mathbin{+} w_{child} \cdot (1 - CPF_i)}
$$ {#eq-two-seater-score}

$$
S_{4s,i} = w_{hs} \cdot (1 - HSF_i) {\mathbin{+} w_{age} \cdot (1 - AAF_i)} + w_{child} \cdot CPF_i + \beta_{child} \cdot \mathbf{1}\{CPF_i > 0.2\}
$$ {#eq-four-seater-score}

where component factors are defined in [Appendix A.7](#sec-ev-type-selection-factors-appendix).

EV type assignment follows score differences:

$$
\widetilde{EV\_type}_i = \begin{cases}
\text{2-seater} & \text{if } S_{2s,i} - S_{4s,i} > \tau_{EV} \\
\text{4-seater} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-ev-type-assignment}

where $\tau_{EV}$ is the minimum score gap required to assign a trip to the 2-seater class; all remaining cases default to the 4-seater class, ensuring exhaustive binary assignment. The underlying implementation evaluates a three-way partition including an intermediate mixed class ($\lvert S_{2s,i} - S_{4s,i} \rvert \leq \tau_{EV}$). In the reported scenario results, regional vehicle-type proportions are fixed allocation assumptions; the OA-level component exercise in Grid 4 does not estimate these trip-weighted proportions.


*Stage 8: Integrated Analysis and Total Substitution Assessment*

Substitution outputs are aggregated across purposes, origins, and destinations.

Theoretical substitution share before capacity assessment:

$$
RR = \frac{\sum_{i,j,p} N_{ij}^{(p)}}{\sum_{i,j{,}{p}} f_{ij}^{{(}{p}{)}}} \cdot 100\%
$$ {#eq-replacement-rate}

where the numerator represents access-qualified, purpose-weighted potential trip volume before capacity assessment, and the denominator represents retained baseline car-person-trip demand. The capacity-sufficient share is reported separately using $V_{\mathrm{screened}}$ as the numerator ([Appendix A.8](#sec-output-aggregation-appendix)).

*Parameter Assessment and Sensitivity Summary*



Parameter assessment comprises seven component-level sensitivity grids and comparisons with external evidence. Scottish MOT-observed BEV cohort counts from the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) provide postcode-area comparison outcomes, Registers of Scotland housing-market statistics (labelled HPI in the component workflows)[^data-hpi] supply covariates, and YouGov/Char.gy survey evidence [@Char.gyYouGov2025] informs demographic scoring assumptions. The 70/30 demographic--home-charging blend, 20/80 accommodation--parking blend and 1.6 interaction multiplier are specified modelling assumptions. [Appendix B](#app-sensitivity-calibration) reports the scoring specifications, samples and diagnostic outcomes applicable to the grids (@tbl-sensitivity-calibration; @tbl-sensitivity-extended), alongside separate sensitivity analyses of the final substitution estimates and purpose ordering.

## Methodological Caveats

Four simplifying assumptions underpin the framework, each discussed in the subsection where it applies most directly: symmetric round-trip evaluation (Core Feasibility Logic), independent trip analysis (Stage 3), representative charger power (Stage 4), and average daily demand for capacity checks (Stage 4). The framework quantifies technical suitability under an assumed demographic market screen rather than behavioural intent, since census-derived indicators capture structural characteristics associated with EV uptake but cannot observe household purchase decisions directly. Substitution outputs should therefore be read as potentials under favourable conditions [@Axsen2013; @Lane2007].

A further source of uncertainty enters upstream, through the origin-destination travel matrices. The aggregate trip rate, purpose allocations and mode shares are survey-informed, but individual zone-to-zone flows are generated by a gravity model. Sensitivity analysis evaluates the substitution volume in @eq-trip-conversion under alternative distance-decay coefficients, AP-band limits and purpose weights on a common routed-trip population. Each scenario includes a charging-capacity assessment based on its station demand. The decay diagnostic multiplies the magnitude of each purpose's negative coefficient by 0.5--1.5 and renormalises within origin-purpose groups, preserving their trip production. The distance used in reweighting is the parent pre-jitter distance: the stored child-record distance is multiplied by its verified integer split multiplicity. This reweights the fixed routed-trip population. AP-band scenarios vary the lower and upper limits, and purpose-weight scenarios multiply the retained $W$ values by 0.75--1.25, capped at one. Results are reported in @tbl-band-edge-headline. These separate families do not constitute a joint uncertainty interval. Destination attractiveness, omitted destinations, route-generation uncertainty and peak charging conditions are not bounded by the decay experiment. Proportional demand changes leave theoretical shares unchanged only with fixed eligibility, but they can change capacity-sufficient shares because charger supply is fixed. The own-data chaining scenarios in [Appendix B.6](#sec-chaining-sensitivity) address a different, explicitly restricted source of uncertainty.


# Findings and Discussion {#sec-findings}

To facilitate interactive exploration of the spatially resolved outputs, the full dataset underpinning these findings, including interactive maps of adoption propensity, charging accessibility, and feasibility outcomes, can be viewed online via the project dashboard: <https://wangzhao0217.github.io/zev-up.github.io/>.



```{r}
#| label: load-regional-data
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| output: false
library(jsonlite)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
# Load all 7 regional summaries
regions <- c("HITRANS", "Nestrans", "SESTRAN", "SPT", "SWESTRANS", "Tactran", "ZetTrans")
regional_data <- list()

# Create display name mapping (for paper text) vs code names (for file paths)
format_region_name <- function(region) {
    # Convert all-caps region names to Title Case for display
    name_map <- c(
        "HITRANS" = "Hitrans",
        "SESTRAN" = "Sestran",
        "SPT" = "Spt",
        "SWESTRANS" = "Swestrans",
        "ZetTrans" = "ZetTrans",
        "Nestrans" = "Nestrans",
        "Tactran" = "Tactran"
    )
    ifelse(region %in% names(name_map), name_map[region], region)
}

for (region in regions) {
    file_path <- opath(region, paste0(region, "_comprehensive_summary.json"))
    if (file.exists(file_path)) {
        regional_data[[region]] <- fromJSON(file_path)
        cat(paste("Loaded:", region, "\n"))
    } else {
        warning(paste("Missing summary file for", region, "at path:", file_path))
    }
}

# Verify data loaded
cat(paste("\nTotal regions loaded:", length(regional_data), "\n"))

# Filter to only regions with loaded data (for tables)
available_regions <- regions[regions %in% names(regional_data)]

# Calculate Scotland-wide totals (use vapply for robust numeric vectors)
scotland_totals <- list(
    total_baseline_trips = sum(vapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) {
        val <- x$conversion_potential$total_baseline_trips
        if (is.null(val)) 0 else as.numeric(val)
    }, numeric(1)), na.rm = TRUE),
    total_conversion_potential = sum(vapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) {
        val <- x$conversion_potential$final_conversion_potential
        if (is.null(val)) 0 else as.numeric(val)
    }, numeric(1)), na.rm = TRUE),
    total_demographic_areas = sum(vapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) {
        val <- x$data_coverage$demographic_areas
        if (is.null(val)) 0 else as.numeric(val)
    }, numeric(1)), na.rm = TRUE),
    total_charging_locations = sum(vapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) {
        val <- x$data_coverage$charging_locations
        if (is.null(val)) 0 else as.numeric(val)
    }, numeric(1)), na.rm = TRUE),
    total_routes = sum(vapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) {
        val <- x$data_coverage$routes
        if (is.null(val)) 0 else as.numeric(val)
    }, numeric(1)), na.rm = TRUE)
)


# Verify totals calculated
cat("\nScotland-wide totals:\n")
cat(paste("  Daily baseline trips:", format(scotland_totals$total_baseline_trips, big.mark = ","), "\n"))
cat(paste("  Substitution potential:", format(scotland_totals$total_conversion_potential, big.mark = ","), "\n"))
cat(paste("  Demographic areas:", format(scotland_totals$total_demographic_areas, big.mark = ","), "\n"))

scotland_totals$conversion_rate_pct <- ifelse(scotland_totals$total_baseline_trips > 0,
    (scotland_totals$total_conversion_potential / scotland_totals$total_baseline_trips) * 100,
    0
)

# Calculate weighted averages for percentages
weighted_means <- function(values, weights) {
    values_num <- as.numeric(unlist(values))
    weights_num <- as.numeric(unlist(weights))
    sum(values_num * weights_num) / sum(weights_num)
}

# Adoption propensity weighted by demographic areas (robust numeric)
adoption_weights <- vapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) {
    val <- x$data_coverage$demographic_areas
    if (is.null(val)) 0 else as.numeric(val)
}, numeric(1))
scotland_totals$mean_adoption <- weighted_means(
    sapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) x$adoption_analysis$mean_adoption_propensity),
    adoption_weights
)

# Home charging weighted by demographic areas
scotland_totals$mean_home_charging <- weighted_means(
    sapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) x$adoption_analysis$mean_home_charging_feasibility),
    adoption_weights
)

# Infrastructure accessibility weighted by demographic areas
scotland_totals$mean_accessibility <- weighted_means(
    sapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) x$infrastructure_analysis$mean_accessibility_score),
    adoption_weights
)

# Frugal EV target areas total - 0.30-0.80 demographic target market (27,480 / 46,359 = 59.3%)
scotland_totals$high_adoption_areas <- sum(r2_oa_counts$target_areas)

cat(paste("  Frugal target areas (0.30-0.80 band):", format(scotland_totals$high_adoption_areas, big.mark = ","), "\n"))
```

```{r}
#| label: calculate-deployment-tiers
#| echo: false
#| output: false
#| message: false
# Extract deployment tiers from regional JSON summaries (already calculated)
cat("\nExtracting deployment feasibility tiers from regional summaries...\n")

# Calculate Scotland-wide totals from regional JSON data
scotland_totals$immediately_feasible <- sum(vapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) {
    val <- x$immediately_feasible_trips
    if (is.null(val)) 0 else as.numeric(val)
}, numeric(1)), na.rm = TRUE)

scotland_totals$constrained_unlockable <- sum(vapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) {
    val <- x$constrained_unlockable_trips
    if (is.null(val)) 0 else as.numeric(val)
}, numeric(1)), na.rm = TRUE)

scotland_totals$currently_infeasible <- sum(vapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) {
    val <- x$currently_infeasible_trips
    if (is.null(val)) 0 else as.numeric(val)
}, numeric(1)), na.rm = TRUE)

# Compute additional_from_charging correctly from constrained_unlockable * unlock_factor
# (JSON field is stale - see abstract block comment for explanation)
scoring_weights_body <- fromJSON("../data/parameters/scoring_weights.json")
unlock_factor_body <- 1 # Conditional capacity-restoration total; no behavioural uptake multiplier.
if (!is.null(unlock_factor_body)) {
    scotland_totals$additional_from_charging <- scotland_totals$constrained_unlockable * unlock_factor_body
} else {
    scotland_totals$additional_from_charging <- 0
}

# Calculate percentages
scotland_totals$immediately_feasible_pct <-
    (scotland_totals$immediately_feasible / scotland_totals$total_baseline_trips) * 100
scotland_totals$constrained_pct <-
    (scotland_totals$constrained_unlockable / scotland_totals$total_baseline_trips) * 100
scotland_totals$infeasible_pct <-
    (scotland_totals$currently_infeasible / scotland_totals$total_baseline_trips) * 100

cat("\n=== Scotland-wide Deployment Tier Summary ===\n")
cat(sprintf(
    "  Screened suitable: %s trips (%.1f%%)\n",
    format(scotland_totals$immediately_feasible, big.mark = ","),
    scotland_totals$immediately_feasible_pct
))
cat(sprintf(
    "  Charging constrained: %s trips (%.1f%%)\n",
    format(scotland_totals$constrained_unlockable, big.mark = ","),
    scotland_totals$constrained_pct
))
cat(sprintf(
    "  Outside screened scenario: %s trips (%.1f%%)\n",
    format(scotland_totals$currently_infeasible, big.mark = ","),
    scotland_totals$infeasible_pct
))
cat(sprintf(
    "  Additional trips from charging investment: %s trips\n",
    format(scotland_totals$additional_from_charging, big.mark = ",")
))

# Print regional breakdown for verification
cat("\nRegional breakdown:\n")
for (region in available_regions) {
    cat(sprintf(
        "  %s: Feasible=%s, Conditional=%s, Infeasible=%s\n",
        region,
        format(regional_data[[region]]$immediately_feasible_trips, big.mark = ","),
        format(regional_data[[region]]$constrained_unlockable_trips, big.mark = ","),
        format(regional_data[[region]]$currently_infeasible_trips, big.mark = ",")
    ))
}
```

## Substitution Potential Across Scotland {#sec-regional-overview}

```{r}
#| label: load-segment-band-r2

seg_band_r2 <- read.csv("../results/validation/segment_band_r2.csv",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
r2_segment_band3080_lower <- seg_band_r2$value[seg_band_r2$metric == "r2_segment_band3080_lower"]
r2_segment_top20_premium <- seg_band_r2$value[seg_band_r2$metric == "r2_segment_top20_premium"]

# Size-controlled Data-Zone / Intermediate-Zone validation of the SAME adoption-

# Band-edge empirical evidence (data-driven changepoint of observed BEV uptake vs
```

Scotland's seven RTPs span island archipelagos, remote Highland communities, and major urban centres, capturing contrasting settlement and infrastructure contexts. @tbl-regional-coverage provides regional scale and core outcomes. The Scotland-wide and regional substitution shares are purpose-weighted theoretical volumes from @eq-trip-conversion, with the capacity-qualified components defined in @eq-trip-classification. These shares are conditional on the 0.3--0.8 adoption-propensity band. The price-segmented comparisons in @sec-adoption-results associate this band with lower-price MOT-tested BEVs from the 2019--2020 cohort (R² = `r sprintf("%.3f", r2_segment_band3080_lower)`) and the above-0.8 band with premium records (R² = `r sprintf("%.3f", r2_segment_top20_premium)`). These raw-count associations are descriptive and do not independently validate the frugal-EV market boundary. In the household-normalised analysis with a house-price control in [Appendix B.7](#sec-ap-threshold-study), the reference band did not improve lower-price MOT prediction over house price alone. Nationally, `r sprintf("%.1f", target_band_pct)`% of Output Areas (`r format(target_band_count, big.mark=",")` of `r format(total_oas, big.mark=",")`) meet the inclusive demographic screen. The alternative-screen comparisons below quantify how much this assumption changes the result.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-regional-coverage
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Regional coverage and core outcomes across Scotland's transport partnerships. Routed records are disaggregated routed observations, not unique zone-to-zone OD pairs. HCF is the home-charging feasibility score. Meeting its threshold indicates assumed home-charging capability, not an observed installed charger."
#| message: false
coverage_table <- data.frame(
    RTP = available_regions,
    `Output Areas (n)` = vapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) as.numeric(x$data_coverage$demographic_areas), numeric(1)),
    `Routed records (n)` = vapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) as.numeric(x$data_coverage$od_pairs), numeric(1)),
    `Baseline Trips per Day` = vapply(regional_data[available_regions], function(x) as.numeric(x$conversion_potential$total_baseline_trips), numeric(1)),
    `Frugal Target OAs (%)` = frugal_target_regional,
    `HCF ≥0.5 OAs (%)` = strong_charging_regional,
    `Poor Infrastructure OAs (%)` = infra_regional,
    `Substitution Potential (%)` = conversion_regional,
    check.names = FALSE
)

# Sort by baseline trips in descending order
coverage_table <- coverage_table[order(coverage_table$`Baseline Trips per Day`, decreasing = TRUE), ]

# Add totals row
totals_row <- data.frame(
    RTP = "Scotland",
    `Output Areas (n)` = sum(coverage_table$`Output Areas (n)`),
    `Routed records (n)` = sum(coverage_table$`Routed records (n)`),
    `Baseline Trips per Day` = sum(coverage_table$`Baseline Trips per Day`),
    `Frugal Target OAs (%)` = (scotland_totals$high_adoption_areas / scotland_totals$total_demographic_areas) * 100,
    `HCF ≥0.5 OAs (%)` = scotland_strong_charging_pct,
    `Poor Infrastructure OAs (%)` = weighted.mean(infra_regional, regional_oa_counts),
    `Substitution Potential (%)` = scotland_totals$conversion_rate_pct,
    check.names = FALSE
)

coverage_table_with_totals <- rbind(coverage_table, totals_row)
coverage_display <- coverage_table_with_totals
if (knitr::is_latex_output() || knitr::is_html_output()) {
    mark_format <- if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "latex" else "html"
    for (col in seq_len(ncol(coverage_display))) {
        values <- if (col == 1) {
            as.character(coverage_table_with_totals[[col]])
        } else if (col <= 4) {
            format(round(coverage_table_with_totals[[col]]), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
        } else {
            sprintf("%.1f", coverage_table_with_totals[[col]])
        }
        coverage_display[[col]] <- kableExtra::cell_spec(
            values,
            format = mark_format, color = "black"
        )
    }
}

if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
    kable(
        coverage_display,
        col.names = gsub("%", "\\%", colnames(coverage_display), fixed = TRUE),
        escape = FALSE,
        format = "latex",
        longtable = FALSE,
        digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1),
        format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
        align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
        row.names = FALSE,
        booktabs = TRUE
    ) |>
        kable_styling(font_size = 8) |>
        column_spec(1, width = "1.3cm") |>
        column_spec(2, width = "1.65cm") |>
        column_spec(3, width = "1.65cm") |>
        column_spec(4, width = "1.65cm") |>

        column_spec(6, width = "1.65cm") |>
        column_spec(7, width = "1.65cm") |>
        column_spec(8, width = "1.65cm")
} else if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
    kable(
        coverage_display,
        escape = FALSE,
        digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1),
        format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
        align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
        row.names = FALSE
    ) |>
        kable_styling(font_size = 10, full_width = TRUE) |>
        column_spec(1, width = "7em") |>
        column_spec(2, width = "8em") |>
        column_spec(3, width = "8em") |>
        column_spec(4, width = "8em") |>
        column_spec(5, width = "8em") |>
        column_spec(6, width = "8em") |>
        column_spec(7, width = "8em") |>
        column_spec(8, width = "8em")
} else {
    kable(
        coverage_table_with_totals,
        digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1),

        row.names = FALSE
    )
}
```





Range alone admits `r r2_pct(r2_metrics$range_volume)`\% of the retained local-trip population. This is not the share of all Scottish car travel: the generator's spatial support limits the available long-distance tail. @tbl-demographic-screen separates this distance diagnostic from charging access, capacity and the AP assumption. All comparisons use the same `r format(round(r2_metrics$baseline_volume), big.mark=",")` car-person trips per day. Station demand and capacity sufficiency depend on whether the AP screen is applied. Rows without purpose weighting omit the purpose-suitability adjustment, whereas the purpose-weighted rows retain the stated behavioural suitability assumptions and are not purely physical feasibility measures.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demographic-screen
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Paired technical and demographic-screen comparisons. Entries are percentages of the same retained car-person-trip denominator. Pre-access includes range and, where applicable, AP and purpose weighting. Theoretical N additionally requires charging access (Pre-access minus Access excluded); capacity-sufficient and capacity-constrained volumes partition N. Rows are alternative scenarios, not additive components; shares are rounded independently."
r2_comparison <- read.csv(file.path(r2_results_dir, "technical_comparison.csv"))
r2_comparison$purpose_weighted <- tolower(r2_comparison$purpose_weighted) == "true"
r2_comparison <- aggregate(
    cbind(
        baseline_volume, screened_pre_access_volume, access_excluded_volume,
        potential_volume, immediate_volume, conditional_volume
    ) ~ screen + purpose_weighted,
    r2_comparison, sum
)
# Every paired row is a separate loading scenario on the same population.
r2_tol <- 1e-10 * pmax(1, r2_comparison$baseline_volume)
stopifnot(
    nrow(r2_comparison) == 4L,
    all(abs(r2_comparison$baseline_volume - r2_metrics$baseline_volume) <= r2_tol),
    all(abs(r2_comparison$potential_volume - r2_comparison$immediate_volume - r2_comparison$conditional_volume) <= r2_tol),
    all(abs(r2_comparison$screened_pre_access_volume - r2_comparison$potential_volume - r2_comparison$access_excluded_volume) <= r2_tol)
)
r2_comparison$Assessment <- paste(
    r2_comparison$screen,
    ifelse(r2_comparison$purpose_weighted, "(purpose weighted)", "(without purpose weighting)")
)
r2_display <- data.frame(
    Assessment = r2_comparison$Assessment,
    `Pre-access` = 100 * r2_comparison$screened_pre_access_volume / r2_comparison$baseline_volume,
    `Access excluded` = 100 * r2_comparison$access_excluded_volume / r2_comparison$baseline_volume,
    `Theoretical N` = 100 * r2_comparison$potential_volume / r2_comparison$baseline_volume,
    `Capacity sufficient` = 100 * r2_comparison$immediate_volume / r2_comparison$baseline_volume,
    `Capacity constrained` = 100 * r2_comparison$conditional_volume / r2_comparison$baseline_volume,
    check.names = FALSE
)
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
    r2_headers <- c(
        "Assessment",
        "\\shortstack[r]{Pre-\\\\access}",
        "\\shortstack[r]{Access\\\\excluded}",
        "\\shortstack[r]{Theoretical\\\\N}",
        "\\shortstack[r]{Capacity\\\\sufficient}",
        "\\shortstack[r]{Capacity\\\\constrained}"
    )
    r2_full_width_table(r2_display, digits = 1, font_size = 9, first_column_width = "6.2cm", col.names = r2_headers, escape = FALSE)
} else {
    r2_full_width_table(r2_display, digits = 1, font_size = 9, first_column_width = "6.2cm")
}
```

Charging-access exclusions account for `r r2_pct(r2_metrics$access_excluded_volume)`\% of baseline demand after purpose weighting and the AP and range screens, and are reported separately from the screen/purpose residual. Public-capacity shortfalls account for `r r2_pct(r2_metrics$conditional_volume)`\% of baseline demand: these trips meet the access rules but fail required origin capacity when home charging is unavailable, destination capacity for 40--80 km trips, or both. Before access is considered, the demographic screen excludes `r r2_pct(r2_metrics$excluded_low_volume)` percentage points below 0.30 and `r r2_pct(r2_metrics$excluded_high_volume)` above 0.80.


### Regional overview and core results





@fig-scotland-adoption-propensity demonstrates spatial heterogeneity in adoption propensity. High-propensity zones concentrate in suburban and peri-urban belts with professional employment, detached housing with off-street parking, and multi-car ownership. Low-propensity areas cluster in dense urban cores with flatted accommodation and social housing, and in remote rural communities where economic constraints and limited charging access constrain uptake.


![Spatial distribution of EV adoption propensity across Scotland's regions (0–1 scale). Values closer to 1 (deep blue) indicate the highest propensity, while values closer to 0 (deep red) indicate the lowest.](figures/adoption_map.png){#fig-scotland-adoption-propensity}


@tbl-demographic-components decomposes this pattern into component scores, revealing clearer regional contrasts. ZetTrans records the highest housing and car-ownership scores, consistent with detached housing, parking availability, and strong vehicle dependence in Shetland. Sestran records the highest social-grade and education scores, whilst SPT records the lowest housing and car-ownership scores, consistent with a larger share of dense urban and flatted neighbourhoods. More rural and island regions therefore combine stronger parking-related feasibility with weaker socioeconomic readiness, whereas the eastern urban-professional regions combine stronger socioeconomic scores with weaker housing-related feasibility. The standard deviations also show that within-region heterogeneity is substantial, especially in SPT, Sestran, and Nestrans, reinforcing the value of Output Area analysis over regional averages.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demographic-components
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Regional demographic component scores (mean and standard deviation) underlying adoption propensity calculations. All scores normalised to [0,1] scale. Higher values indicate greater EV adoption suitability for each dimension."
#| message: false
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

# Calculate demographic component statistics for each region
component_stats <- list()

for (region in available_regions) {
    gpkg_path <- opath(region, "adoption_propensity_categorized.gpkg")
    if (file.exists(gpkg_path)) {
        region_data <- st_read(gpkg_path, quiet = TRUE) |> st_drop_geometry()

        component_stats[[region]] <- data.frame(
            Region = format_region_name(region),
            `Social Grade` = sprintf(
                "%.3f (%.3f)",
                mean(region_data$social_grade_score, na.rm = TRUE),
                sd(region_data$social_grade_score, na.rm = TRUE)
            ),
            `Education` = sprintf(
                "%.3f (%.3f)",
                mean(region_data$education_score, na.rm = TRUE),
                sd(region_data$education_score, na.rm = TRUE)
            ),
            `Car Ownership` = sprintf(
                "%.3f (%.3f)",
                mean(region_data$car_ownership_score, na.rm = TRUE),
                sd(region_data$car_ownership_score, na.rm = TRUE)
            ),
            `Housing` = sprintf(
                "%.3f (%.3f)",
                mean(region_data$housing_score, na.rm = TRUE),
                sd(region_data$housing_score, na.rm = TRUE)
            ),
            check.names = FALSE
        )
    }
}

demographic_table <- bind_rows(component_stats)

library(kableExtra)

if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
    kable(demographic_table,
        align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
        row.names = FALSE,
        booktabs = TRUE
    ) |>
        kable_styling(font_size = 9, latex_options = c("hold_position")) |>
        column_spec(1, width = "2.5cm") |>
        column_spec(2, width = "3cm") |>
        column_spec(3, width = "3cm") |>
        column_spec(4, width = "3cm") |>
        column_spec(5, width = "3cm")
} else if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
    kable(demographic_table,
        align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
        row.names = FALSE
    ) |>
        kable_styling(full_width = TRUE)
} else {
    kable(demographic_table,
        align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
        row.names = FALSE
    )
}
```


@fig-oa-distribution-violin extends this evidence with OA-level distributions of (a) adoption propensity and (b) home charging feasibility, revealing inter-regional contrasts and substantial within-region heterogeneity. Violin width indicates density of OA scores; embedded boxplots show median and interquartile range.
@fig-oa-adoption indicates that adoption propensity is centred well within the frugal-target range in most regions rather than clustering below its lower boundary. Medians exceed 0.4 in every RTP and are highest in ZetTrans, Hitrans, and Nestrans, whereas SPT remains lowest; this ordering is consistent with stronger suburban-rural housing and car-ownership profiles outside the Glasgow-centred urban core. The violins also show marked within-region heterogeneity, especially in SPT and Sestran, where broad spreads and long upper tails indicate that low-feasibility urban output areas coexist with pockets of much higher propensity.
@fig-oa-hcf shows a clear split around the home-charging feasibility threshold $\tau_{HCF} = 0.5$. ZetTrans and Hitrans are centred above the threshold, Swestrans and Nestrans sit close to it, and SPT remains clearly below it, consistent with dense urban areas having more limited off-street parking and therefore weaker home-charging access.

```{r}
#| label: oa-violin-setup
#| echo: false
#| include: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)

# Load OA-level data for all regions
oa_data_list <- list()
for (region in available_regions) {
    gpkg_path <- opath(region, "adoption_propensity_categorized.gpkg")
    if (file.exists(gpkg_path)) {
        region_sf <- st_read(gpkg_path, quiet = TRUE) |>
            st_drop_geometry() |>
            select(final_adoption_propensity, home_charging_feasibility) |>
            mutate(Region = format_region_name(region))
        oa_data_list[[region]] <- region_sf
    }
}
oa_data <- bind_rows(oa_data_list)

# Order regions by median adoption propensity
region_order <- oa_data |>
    group_by(Region) |>
    summarise(med = median(final_adoption_propensity, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    arrange(med) |>
    pull(Region)
oa_data$Region <- factor(oa_data$Region, levels = region_order)

# Colour palette
region_colours <- setNames(
    RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(7, "Set2"),
    region_order
)
```

@fig-adoption-charging-scatter presents the Scotland-wide bivariate distribution across 46,359 output areas and demonstrates a strong positive association between adoption propensity and home-charging feasibility. The diagonal concentration of points indicates systematic co-variation: output areas with higher adoption propensity generally exhibit higher home-charging feasibility, while low values on one dimension are typically accompanied by low values on the other. The shaded intersection identifies Output Areas within the assumed AP target band that also meet the modelled home-charging threshold. It does not establish installed charging availability or trip-level suitability, which are assessed separately. Because home-charging feasibility contributes to AP, part of the plotted association is built into the score.

```{r}
#| label: fig-adoption-charging-scatter
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Relationship between adoption propensity and home charging feasibility across Scotland's Output Areas. Vertical dashed lines indicate frugal EV target market boundaries (0.3–0.8); horizontal dashed line marks the binary feasibility threshold ($\\tau_{HCF} = 0.5$)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| message: false
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)

# Ensure format_region_name function is available
if (!exists("format_region_name")) {
    format_region_name <- function(region) {
        name_map <- c(
            "HITRANS" = "Hitrans",
            "SESTRAN" = "Sestran",
            "SPT" = "Spt",
            "SWESTRANS" = "Swestrans",
            "ZetTrans" = "ZetTrans",
            "Nestrans" = "Nestrans",
            "Tactran" = "Tactran"
        )
        ifelse(region %in% names(name_map), name_map[region], region)
    }
}

# Reuse the validated inventory used by the national and regional OA tables.
scatter_data <- all_adoption_data |>
    mutate(Region = format_region_name(region))
stopifnot(nrow(scatter_data) == total_oas)
cor_value <- cor(
    scatter_data$final_adoption_propensity,
    scatter_data$home_charging_feasibility
)

# The shaded intersection is the home-chargeable subset of the AP-only target.
scatter_target <- r2_target_band(scatter_data$final_adoption_propensity)
stopifnot(sum(scatter_target) == target_band_count)
home_chargeable_target <- sum(scatter_target & scatter_data$home_charging_feasibility >= 0.5)

# Create scatter plot
ggplot(scatter_data, aes(x = final_adoption_propensity, y = home_charging_feasibility, color = Region)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.2, stroke = 0.3) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", size = 0.8) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0.3, linetype = "dashed", color = "blue", size = 0.8) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0.8, linetype = "dashed", color = "blue", size = 0.8) +
    annotate("rect",
        xmin = 0.3, xmax = 0.8, ymin = 0.5, ymax = 1,
        alpha = 0.1, fill = "green"
    ) +
    annotate("text",
        x = 0.55, y = 0.95,
        label = sprintf("Home-chargeable target OAs\n%s areas", format(home_chargeable_target, big.mark = ",")),
        color = "darkgreen", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5
    ) +
    annotate("text",
        x = 0.05, y = 0.95,
        label = sprintf("Pearson r (all OAs): %.3f", cor_value),
        size = 4, hjust = 0, fontface = "bold"
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(
        "Sestran" = "#1f77b4", # Deep blue
        "Tactran" = "#ff7f0e", # Deep orange
        "Swestrans" = "#2ca02c", # Deep green
        "Nestrans" = "#d62728", # Deep red
        "Hitrans" = "#9467bd", # Deep purple
        "ZetTrans" = "#8c564b", # Deep brown
        "Spt" = "#e377c2"
    )) + # Deep pink
    labs(
        x = "Final Adoption Propensity (0-1)",
        y = "Home Charging Feasibility (0-1)",
        color = "Region"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        legend.position = "right",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10)
    )
```



To interpret the demographic structure, @fig-pca-biplot-spt presents SPT as representative. Each point is an Output Area positioned on the two leading principal components, which summarise the demographic indicators into the two directions of greatest variation, so areas plotted close together have similar demographic profiles; the loading arrows point in the direction in which each indicator increases, and their length indicates how strongly that indicator contributes. Three groups, defined by the propensity cut-offs, are shown: Below Minimum (AP < 0.3, red), outside the lower screen; Feasible Range (0.3 ≤ AP ≤ 0.8, green), within the assumed frugal-EV market screen; and Above Maximum (AP > 0.8, blue), outside the upper screen. These labels are scenario assignments, not observed household choices. The three bands are demographically stratified along the leading principal component, with high-propensity areas toward higher housing and car-ownership scores, consistent with off-street parking and multi-vehicle households, and low-propensity areas where housing is constrained and socioeconomic indicators are lower; they overlap, however, rather than forming discrete clusters, so the bands are best understood as a behaviourally motivated partition of a demographic gradient. The partition is robust to the cut-off choice, with 93% of Output Areas unchanged under $\pm 0.05$ shifts of either edge.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
```

## What Drives Feasibility

Understanding which demographic dimensions covary clarifies how household characteristics translate into adoption feasibility. @fig-adoption-correlation-network presents pairwise Pearson correlations among demographic components, displayed as a hierarchically clustered bubble correlogram. Each cell shows the pairwise Pearson correlation between two components; circle colour encodes the sign and strength of the correlation (red positive, blue negative, deeper colour stronger) and circle size encodes its magnitude, so large dark-red circles mark strongly co-varying pairs. Reordering by hierarchical clustering places related components adjacently so that blocks of mutually correlated indicators become visible along the diagonal.

The correlation structure indicates a coherent household affluence-mobility block: housing, car ownership, home charging, economic activity, social grade, and adoption propensity are predominantly positively associated. Within this block, social grade correlates strongly with education (r = 0.89) and moderately with car ownership (r = 0.47). Population density shows weak associations with housing (r = 0.07) and car ownership (r = 0.06), indicating that density alone does not predict these adoption drivers at Output Area resolution. Household composition is positively associated with adoption propensity (r = 0.61), reflecting higher family-household shares in areas that also exhibit stronger car ownership and more favourable accommodation profiles. Clustering identifies three groups: socioeconomic status (social grade, education, car ownership), housing-geography (housing, density), and demographic structure (age, household composition, economic activity).

```{r}
#| label: fig-adoption-correlation-network
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Correlogram of the demographic components contributing to adoption propensity. Colours indicate positive (red) and negative (blue) correlations, while circle size represents the strength of the relationship, with larger circles indicating stronger correlations."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-pos: "H" 
#| fig-height: 10
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(corrplot)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
library(RColorBrewer)

# Load all regional adoption data and combine
adoption_components_list <- list()
for (region in available_regions) {
    adoption_file <- opath(region, "adoption_propensity_categorized.gpkg")
    if (file.exists(adoption_file)) {
        region_sf <- st_read(adoption_file, quiet = TRUE) |>
            st_drop_geometry() |>
            select(
                social_grade_score, education_score, car_ownership_score,
                housing_score, age_score, economic_activity_score,
                household_composition_score, population_density_score,
                final_adoption_propensity, home_charging_feasibility
            )
        adoption_components_list[[region]] <- region_sf
    }
}
adoption_components <- bind_rows(adoption_components_list)

# Rename for cleaner labels
colnames(adoption_components) <- c(
    "Social Grade", "Education", "Car Ownership", "Housing",
    "Age", "Economic Activity", "Household Type", "Population Density",
    "Final Adoption", "Home Charging"
)

# Calculate correlation matrix with significance testing
cor_matrix <- cor(adoption_components, use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "pearson")

# Calculate p-values for correlations
cor_p_values <- matrix(NA, nrow = ncol(adoption_components), ncol = ncol(adoption_components))
n_samples <- nrow(adoption_components)

for (i in 1:ncol(adoption_components)) {
    for (j in 1:ncol(adoption_components)) {
        if (i != j) {
            test_result <- cor.test(adoption_components[[i]], adoption_components[[j]],
                use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "pearson"
            )
            cor_p_values[i, j] <- test_result$p.value
        }
    }
}

# Give the p-value matrix the same dimnames as the correlation matrix and a
# non-NA diagonal so corrplot significance/cross marking (p.mat) renders.
dimnames(cor_p_values) <- dimnames(cor_matrix)
diag(cor_p_values) <- 0

# Create significance matrix (p < 0.01: ***, p < 0.05: **, p < 0.1: *)
sig_matrix <- ifelse(cor_p_values < 0.001, "***",
    ifelse(cor_p_values < 0.01, "**",
        ifelse(cor_p_values < 0.05, "*", "")
    )
)

# Perform hierarchical clustering manually to control the process
dist_matrix <- as.dist(1 - abs(cor_matrix))
hc <- hclust(dist_matrix, method = "complete")
var_order <- hc$order

# Reorder matrices according to clustering
cor_matrix_ordered <- cor_matrix[var_order, var_order]
cor_p_values_ordered <- cor_p_values[var_order, var_order]

# Plot correlation network - simplified to avoid corrplot bugs
corrplot(cor_matrix_ordered,
    method = "circle",
    type = "upper",
    order = "original",
    tl.col = "black",
    tl.srt = 45,
    tl.cex = 0.9,
    cl.cex = 0.8,
    col = colorRampPalette(c("#2166AC", "#F7F7F7", "#B2182B"))(200),
    diag = FALSE,
    p.mat = cor_p_values_ordered,
    sig.level = 0.05,
    insig = "pch",
    pch = 4,
    pch.cex = 1.6,
    pch.col = "grey30"
)

# Cross-marking of non-significant correlations is enabled via p.mat/insig
# (pch = 4 draws a cross where p >= 0.05).

# Add title
title(
    main = "Demographic Component Correlation Network\n(Hierarchically clustered)",
    cex.main = 1.0, line = -1
)
```



### Adoption propensity and demographics {#sec-adoption-results}

```{r}
#| label: mot-fy-validation
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# First-use-year BEV validation using 2022 Census scores.
# Produces the temporal-delta plot (Δ propensity 2022-2011 vs first-use BEV
# 2019–2020) and two price-segmented scatter plots (top-20% vs premium EVs;
# 30–80% band vs lower-price EVs) plus the HPI independent-check figure.

library(reticulate)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Ensure the ev_model Python environment is used
# Python is selected by RETICULATE_PYTHON in reproduce.py.
```

External consistency checks evaluate whether composite adoption-propensity scores correspond with observed area-level BEV uptake. The primary comparison relates household-weighted 2022 Output Area AP scores, aggregated to Data Zones, to privately kept licensed BEVs per 1,000 households in 2025 Q4, derived from DfT VEH0145. The AP inputs match those used in the substitution analysis. Across `r format(ap_dz_n, big.mark=",")` Data Zones with available BEV counts, the Spearman correlation is `r sprintf("%.3f", ap_dz_rho)`. After adjustment for the SIMD-derived affordability measure $A_{it}$, the partial correlation is `r sprintf("%.3f", ap_dz_partial)`. Because AP combines demographic and home-charging indicators, this association does not identify their separate contributions.

Intermediate-Zone comparisons aggregate BEV counts, household totals and household-weighted AP scores over the same constituent Data Zones with available counts. Across `r format(ap_iz_n, big.mark=",")` Intermediate Zones, the correlation is `r sprintf("%.3f", ap_iz_rho)`; the observed constituent Data Zones represent `r sprintf("%.1f", ap_iz_coverage_pct)`% of households in those zones. Restricting the comparison to the `r format(ap_iz_complete_n, big.mark=",")` Intermediate Zones with complete count coverage gives a correlation of `r sprintf("%.3f", ap_iz_complete_rho)`. Missing counts are not treated as zero. These comparisons describe associations within the observed samples; differences in coverage and sample composition limit comparisons between geographic scales. They do not independently validate frugal-EV substitution.

Supplementary postcode-area comparisons examine aggregate patterns. @fig-mot-fy-temporal compares the 2011--2022 change in summed AP with MOT-derived counts of electric-coded vehicles first used in 2019--2020 (r = `r sprintf("%.3f", cor_adoption_bev$estimate)`, R² = `r sprintf("%.3f", r2_primary)`). @fig-hpi-propensity-2022 compares summed 2022 AP with cumulative residential property transaction values through 2022, showing a correlation of `r sprintf("%.3f", cor_hpi_adoption$estimate)`. Because these postcode-area totals depend on area size as well as underlying demographic characteristics, the comparisons provide descriptive context rather than evidence that demographic composition has been distinguished from population scale.


::: {#fig-validation-grid layout-ncol=2}

![](figures/mot_temporal.png){#fig-mot-fy-temporal width=90%}

![](figures/house_price.png){#fig-hpi-propensity-2022 width=90%}

Postcode-area comparisons with MOT-derived electric-vehicle counts for the 2019--2020 first-use cohort and cumulative residential property transaction values through 2022.
:::

[]{#sec-threshold-validation}

These comparisons assess the geographical correspondence of the AP index with existing BEV uptake. The $0.30 \leq AP \leq 0.80$ range serves a separate purpose: it defines the demographic target segment evaluated in the frugal-EV screening scenario.
Areas below the lower boundary have lower mean housing-suitability and social-grade scores than those within the band: 0.422 versus 0.636 and 0.277 versus 0.423, respectively. These differences indicate less favourable modelled socioeconomic and home-charging conditions, rather than demonstrating that all households below the boundary are unable to adopt or operate an EV.
Areas above the upper boundary have a higher mean car-ownership score than those within the band, 0.729 versus 0.460, and `r sprintf("%.1f", high_prop_hcf_pct)`\% of Output Areas meet the modelled home-charging feasibility threshold ($HCF_i \geq \tau_{HCF}$, with $\tau_{HCF}=0.5$). Excluding these areas focuses the scenario on an intermediate-readiness segment rather than the highest-scoring areas. This is a market-screening assumption, not evidence that higher-AP households would not consider a frugal EV. Because demographic readiness and home-charging feasibility contribute directly to AP, component differences across bands partly reflect the construction of the index rather than independent confirmation of distinct market segments.
The selected band includes `r format(target_band_count, big.mark=",")` Output Areas (`r sprintf("%.1f", target_band_pct)`% of all OAs), of which `r sprintf("%.1f", target_hcf_pct)`% meet the modelled home-charging feasibility threshold. These statistics describe the geographical coverage and modelled charging characteristics of the selected scenario segment. They do not identify individual households' purchasing intentions. The sensitivity of the theoretical and capacity-sufficient substitution shares to alternative band boundaries is reported in @tbl-band-edge-headline.

Price-segmented MOT records provide exploratory context for the market-screening assumption (@fig-segment-grid). Among vehicles with matched model-family price proxies, the premium category comprises those whose proxy price exceeds 1.5 times an annualised earnings reference for the first-use year. This reference is 52 times UK median gross weekly earnings for full-time employee jobs, rounded to the nearest pound before annualisation [@ONSASHE2025Earnings]. The remaining matched vehicles are classified as lower-price; unmatched vehicles remain unclassified. Postcode-area sums of AP scores for OAs above 0.80 are associated with premium BEV counts (R² = `r sprintf("%.3f", r2_segment_top20_premium)` across `r band_edge_fits$premium_n[1]` matched postcode areas), while sums across the target band ($0.30 \leq AP \leq 0.80$) track lower-price counts (R² = `r sprintf("%.3f", r2_segment_band3080_lower)` across `r band_edge_fits$lower_n[1]` areas).

::: {#fig-segment-grid layout-ncol=2}

![](figures/premium_segment.png){#fig-segment-top20 width=90%}

![](figures/lower_price_segment.png){#fig-segment-band3080 width=90%}

Postcode-area consistency checks using price-segmented MOT records: (a) AP > 0.8 versus premium BEV counts, and (b) $0.30 \leq AP \leq 0.80$ band versus lower-price BEV counts.
:::




### Trip purpose suitability and substitution rates

```{r}
#| label: compute-purpose-rates
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# Calculate Scotland-wide substitution rates by purpose
regions <- c("HITRANS", "Nestrans", "SESTRAN", "SPT", "SWESTRANS", "Tactran", "ZetTrans")

all_purpose_data <- do.call(rbind, lapply(regions, function(r) {
    path <- opath(r, "replaceable_trips_by_purpose.csv")
    if (file.exists(path)) {
        df <- read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
        names(df)[1] <- "purpose"
        df$region <- r
        df
    } else {
        NULL
    }
}))

scotland_purpose_rates <- all_purpose_data |>
    group_by(purpose) |>
    summarise(
        total_car = sum(car_trips, na.rm = TRUE),
        total_replaceable = sum(replaceable_trips, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(rate = (total_replaceable / total_car) * 100) |>
    arrange(desc(rate))

top_volume_purposes <- scotland_purpose_rates |>
    arrange(desc(total_replaceable)) |>
    head(2)

# Extract specific purpose rates for inline use
get_rate <- function(purpose_name) {
    rate <- scotland_purpose_rates$rate[scotland_purpose_rates$purpose == purpose_name]
    if (length(rate) == 0) {
        return(0)
    }
    return(rate)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: extract-top-bottom-purposes
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
top3 <- head(scotland_purpose_rates, 3)
bottom3 <- tail(scotland_purpose_rates, 3)
low2 <- tail(scotland_purpose_rates, 2)
high_vs_low_pct <- ((mean(top3$rate, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(low2$rate, na.rm = TRUE)) - 1) * 100
```

Applying the assigned suitability weights from @tbl-trip-purpose-inputs to the synthetic trip flows yields a twofold variation in substitution rates across the modelled trip purposes. (The two travel-diary purposes not modelled, Go home and Go for a walk, do not appear below.) The highest substitution rates are assigned to `r top3$purpose[1]` (`r sprintf("%.1f", top3$rate[1])`%), `r top3$purpose[2]` (`r sprintf("%.1f", top3$rate[2])`%), and `r top3$purpose[3]` (`r sprintf("%.1f", top3$rate[3])`%), reflecting the higher regularity and predictability ratings specified for routine journeys; at the lower end, `r bottom3$purpose[3]` (`r sprintf("%.1f", bottom3$rate[3])`%), `r bottom3$purpose[2]` (`r sprintf("%.1f", bottom3$rate[2])`%), and `r bottom3$purpose[1]` (`r sprintf("%.1f", bottom3$rate[1])`%) receive lower substitution rates because their assigned parameters reflect lower assumed scheduling consistency and charging compatibility [@Turrentine2007; @Ling2019]. These purpose differences are direct consequences of the assigned weighting framework applied to synthetic travel demand, rather than empirical observations of vehicle dwell or route unfamiliarity within the simulated flows.

Because the suitability scores rest partly on expert-assigned ordinal ratings for regularity, predictability, dwell flexibility, and temporal sensitivity, the stability of the resulting purpose ordering was tested directly in a dedicated robustness analysis reported in [Appendix B](#app-sensitivity-calibration): the three aggregation weights in @eq-trip-purpose-weight were varied across 120 weighting schemes on a restricted simplex, with each weight between 0.10 and 0.80 in increments of 0.05 and weights summing to one, and the ordinal ratings themselves were perturbed with uniform noise in 10,000 Monte Carlo draws per noise level. The suitability ordering that underpins the purpose weights is most stable at the top: commuting and education remain the top-two set in all 19 plausible weighting schemes (within $\pm 0.10$ of the reference weights) and in every $\pm 0.05$ rating-jitter draw, and the top three purposes (adding shopping) are preserved in 94.7% of plausible schemes and 80.8% of jitter draws, with median Kendall $\tau$-b of 0.97 and 0.97 respectively. Stability declines towards the foot of the ordering and under broader perturbations, so the substantive interpretation rests on the rank ordering of the leading purposes rather than on the precise ordinal values assigned to any single purpose.

```{r}
#| label: compute-regional-totals
#| echo: false
regional_totals <- all_purpose_data |>
    group_by(region) |>
    summarise(
        total_car = sum(car_trips, na.rm = TRUE),
        total_replaceable = sum(replaceable_trips, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(rate = (total_replaceable / total_car) * 100) |>

top_volume_regions <- head(regional_totals, 2)
highest_rate_region <- regional_totals |>
    arrange(desc(rate)) |>
```
