| Social Grade Scoring | 2 | 56 | AB=1.0, C1=0.65, C2=0.25, DE=0.0 | Deviation 0.53–0.68 from 84/16 target |
| Home Charging Feasibility | 3 | 1,080 | H=0.92, F=0.22, acc:park=20:80 | Negative correlations; ordinary n=18, partial n=16 |
| EV Type Selection | 4 | 280 | w_hs=0.6, w_age=0.3, w_child=0.1, $\beta$=0.0, $\tau_{child}$=0.1 | 32.8566% two-seater OA assignments; n=46,359 |
| Geographic Multipliers | 5 | 14,406 | Remote=0.70, suburban=1.08 (assumed) | Full factorial; unit mean imposed by normalisation |
| Trip Purpose Weights | 6 | 56 | Scheme A (35/35/30%) | Fourteen-purpose commuting score=0.8575 |
| Interaction Effects | 7 | 16,807 | Assumed synergy=1.6, compound=0.5, peak_age=1.45 | Simplified proxy; magnitudes not estimated |

| 6 | Regularity, predictability and charging-flexibility weights; shopping regularity | 8 schemes × 7 shopping ratings | Sample CV across schemes | 35/35/30% | Commute CV=3.38%; mean-suitability CV=2.10% |
| 7 | Synergy, education/income penalties, compound and peak-age effects | 7 levels for each of 5 parameters | Score-response diagnostic | Assumed synergy=1.6 | No numerical calibration |
: Component-grid parameters and diagnostic metrics. Grid 4 uses the 46,359-OA study inventory; its chi-squared discrepancy and 10% target apply to the same binary subset. Sample definitions and other metric denominators are specified in Appendix B.2. {#tbl-sensitivity-extended}

### Band-Edge Sensitivity {.unnumbered}

The adoption-propensity band edges (0.30 and 0.80) are examined here under alternative specifications. @tbl-band-edge-r2 reports the price-segmented fit against MOT-tested BEV records (2019--2020 cohort) as the edges are varied, and @tbl-band-edge-headline reports the resulting headline substitution share.

| Edges | Lower-price R² | Premium R² |
|---|---|---|
| 0.30 / 0.80 (reference) | `r sprintf("%.3f", band_edge_fits$lower_r2[1])` | `r sprintf("%.3f", band_edge_fits$premium_r2[1])` |
| 0.25 / 0.80 | `r sprintf("%.3f", band_edge_fits$lower_r2[2])` | `r sprintf("%.3f", band_edge_fits$premium_r2[2])` |
| 0.40 / 0.70 | `r sprintf("%.3f", band_edge_fits$lower_r2[3])` | `r sprintf("%.3f", band_edge_fits$premium_r2[3])` |
| 0.20 / 0.90 | `r sprintf("%.3f", band_edge_fits$lower_r2[4])` | `r sprintf("%.3f", band_edge_fits$premium_r2[4])` |
| 0.30 / 0.85 | `r sprintf("%.3f", band_edge_fits$lower_r2[5])` | `r sprintf("%.3f", band_edge_fits$premium_r2[5])` |

: Price-segmented fits under alternative AP-band edges, evaluated with the 2022 Census-derived AP surface and MOT-tested BEV records from the 2019--2020 cohort (matched postcode areas: `r band_edge_fits$lower_n[1]` lower-price, `r band_edge_fits$premium_n[1]` premium). {#tbl-band-edge-r2}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-band-edge-headline
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity of theoretical and capacity-sufficient substitution shares to AP-band limits, distance decay and purpose weights. Both shares use the same retained daily car-person-trip denominator. Decay multipliers preserve origin-purpose productions on fixed routed support; purpose-weight multipliers are capped at one. These are separate scenario families, not a joint uncertainty interval."
r2_scenario_display <- r2_scenario_totals[, c("family", "scenario", "potential_pct", "immediate_pct")]
r2_scenario_display <- r2_scenario_display[order(
    match(r2_scenario_display$family, c(
        "AP band", "Decay multiplier",
        "Purpose-weight multiplier"
    )),
    r2_scenario_display$scenario
), ]
names(r2_scenario_display) <- c("Family", "Setting", "Theoretical N (%)", "Capacity sufficient (%)")

```

The theoretical reference share is `r r2_pct(r2_metrics$potential_volume)`\%, with separate-family outcomes spanning `r sprintf("%.1f--%.1f", r2_envelope[1], r2_envelope[2])`\%. Each theoretical share includes the AP, range and charging-access conditions and the purpose weight. Capacity-sufficient shares additionally account for shared station demand.

## B.2 Component Assessment and Consistency-Check Methodology {#sec-validation-methodology-appendix .unnumbered}

### Data Sources {.unnumbered}

**MOT BEV Records**: The threshold and price-segment analyses use electric-coded vehicles passing an MOT, grouped by first-use cohort (2019--2020). These records describe MOT-observed cohorts rather than a complete new-registration series. The analyses cover 16 Scottish postcode areas before additional matching restrictions, with `r band_edge_fits$lower_n[1]` matched areas in the price-segment comparison. Grid 3 instead uses the latest available test per electric-coded vehicle across all recorded first-use years and test outcomes. Clipping postcode polygons to Scotland retains 18 areas, including CA and NE, without apportioning their whole-postcode BEV counts to the Scottish intersections. Its ordinary comparison therefore includes differences in geographic coverage at the border.

**House-Price Statistics**: Data-Zone sale prices, counts and values aggregated to postcode area. Grid 3 uses summed 2011 transaction values, available for 16 of its 18 postcode areas; CA and NE lack this covariate. The threshold study uses log mean sale price for 2019--2020, separating price level from sales volume. These are area-level housing-market proxies.

**YouGov/Char.gy Survey**: National survey data [@Char.gyYouGov2025] indicating 84% of UK EV owners belong to ABC1 social grades versus 16% C2DE, used to inform and assess the consistency of social grade scoring weights.

MOT counts support component-score comparisons and are reused in the temporal and price-segment checks. Housing-market measures supply covariates, while owner-demographic surveys inform scoring assumptions. DfT small-area BEV counts provide a complementary conventional-BEV benchmark. The threshold analysis uses internal area-holdout comparisons conditional on the fixed reference AP score. Reuse of evidence from model development does not establish independent predictive performance.

### Statistical Methods {.unnumbered}

**Grid 1 (Adoption Propensity)**: Postcode-area sums of min--max-rescaled component scores are compared with MOT BEV counts using Pearson correlation. Scheme A gives a squared correlation of 0.4151 across all six positive score caps. Because the caps uniformly rescale the scores, this statistic cannot identify an optimal cap. A separate diagnostic compares counts of OAs above a threshold with MOT counts; this measures a different outcome from the summed-score comparison. The grid's multiplicative score cap is distinct from the upper AP eligibility boundary in the trip model.

**Grid 3 (Home Charging)**: OA home-charging scores are aggregated by intersection-area weighting to postcode polygons clipped to Scotland. Ordinary correlations compare these means with whole-postcode MOT BEV counts across 18 areas. Partial correlations control for the transaction-value covariate and use the 16 complete cases, excluding CA and NE. For house and flat feasibility scores of 0.92 and 0.22 and accommodation/parking weights of 20/80, the five parking-bonus settings give ordinary correlations from -0.290 to -0.264 and partial correlations from -0.287 to -0.200. Partial-correlation p values range from 0.299 to 0.475. The covariate combines price levels and sales volume; the shared 16-area membership does not make this the same vehicle cohort or housing measure as the threshold study.

**Grid 4 (EV Type Selection)**: The vehicle-assignment grid evaluates all 46,359 study OAs, matched by OA identifier to the 2022 demographic compatibility input. Housing, age and household-composition factors use the configured non-overlapping categories. Eight weighting schemes, seven children-bonus values and five child-presence thresholds give 280 configurations. The component exercise disables Stage 6 filtering and fixes the assignment margin at 0.30 and the two-/four-seater score thresholds at 0.70/0.30. The all-OA two-seater share includes mixed assignments in its denominator. A separate binary-subset share and descriptive chi-squared discrepancy use only two- and four-seater assignments, compared with an assumed 10% two-seater target. These OA diagnostics do not estimate observed vehicle-market shares or the trip-weighted allocation proportions.

**Grid 5 (Geographic Multipliers)**: The full factorial sweep contains 14,406 settings (7 rural, 7 very-rural, 6 remote, 7 suburban and 7 high-density levels). The separate BEV comparison uses 200 draws, choosing each parameter independently and uniformly from its discrete levels with replacement. This is not Latin-hypercube sampling. The exact retained settings are archived because the Python random state was not recorded. Normalisation imposes a mean adjustment of one, while the saved BEV regression fit is identical across all 200 settings. Neither result identifies an optimal multiplier; the reference geographic multipliers remain assumptions.

**Grid 6 (Trip Purpose)**: The grid evaluates fourteen purpose labels using directly specified charging-flexibility ratings. Eight aggregation schemes are combined with seven shopping-regularity ratings. The commuting-score CV across schemes is 3.38%. The CV of scheme-level mean suitability is 2.10%, after averaging over the seven shopping-regularity settings. Both CVs use the sample standard deviation divided by the mean.

**Grid 7 (Interaction Effects)**: The grid evaluates 16,807 configurations of a simplified interaction specification. AP intervals substitute for separate demographic conditions, and the education and income penalty arguments are not applied. Varying the synergy parameter does not change the stored mean adjusted score when compound penalty and peak-age bonus are fixed. No BEV-validation result is available for this exercise. The grid therefore does not estimate the reference interaction multiplier.

## B.3 Component Diagnostics and Parameter Assumptions {#sec-key-calibration-results-appendix .unnumbered}

### Demographic-Weight Diagnostics {.unnumbered}

Across the eight demographic weighting schemes, the squared correlation between summed scores and MOT BEV counts ranges from 0.4128 to 0.4165. This limited variation describes the aggregate association under the grid's scoring implementation. It does not establish robustness of OA eligibility or final substitution volumes.

### Home-Charging Weight Assumptions {.unnumbered}

The reference HCF specification assigns accommodation and parking weights of 0.20 and 0.80. These weights specify the relative contributions of the two components. Grid 3 does not establish this ratio as an empirical optimum or demonstrate a positive association with BEV counts. The separate substantive rationale for including parking access is discussed in Stage 2.

### EV-Type Assignment Diagnostics {.unnumbered}

Under household-size, age and children weights of 0.6, 0.3 and 0.1, with children bonus 0 and child-presence threshold 0.1, Grid 4 assigns 15,232 OAs to two-seaters, 19,982 to four-seaters and 11,145 to the mixed category. Two-seater assignments comprise 32.8566% of the 46,359 OAs. Within the binary subset of 35,214 OAs, the corresponding share is 43.2555%. Across 280 configurations, the all-OA share ranges from 0.9146% to 55.1802%, with 210 configurations exceeding 10%; the binary-subset share ranges from 0.9507% to 63.9523%, with 234 exceeding the assumed 10% target. These results do not support systematic underestimation across configurations. The OA-assignment diagnostics are distinct from the fixed regional trip-allocation assumptions used in the national scenarios.

### Interaction Effect Assumptions {#interaction-effect-corroboration .unnumbered}

The social-grade–education multiplier of 1.6 is a modelling assumption. Gehrke and Reardon [-@Gehrke2021] estimated an interaction between single-family residence and the census-tract share of households earning at least US\$150,000, with public charging-site count included separately (their Table 5). This provides qualitative motivation for considering interactions in EV adoption models. It does not estimate a social-grade–education effect or provide a numerical calibration of the multiplier used here. Grid 7 therefore cannot establish the empirical validity of that value through agreement with this citation.

## B.4 Trip-Purpose Classification Cutoff Calibration {#sec-trip-purpose-cutoff-calibration-appendix .unnumbered}

Trip-purpose class cutoffs were calibrated from model-generated regional purpose substitution outcomes across seven RTPs (84 region-purpose combinations). The resulting classes summarise purpose suitability, while substitution volumes retain the continuous weights in @eq-trip-conversion. The comparison evaluates three procedures: supervised weighted grid search, segmented breakpoint fitting, and weighted-quantile mapping; evaluation used leave-one-region-out cross-validation with trip-volume weighting and 1,000 bootstrap resamples. The selected specification (weighted-quantile mapping) yields $W^{(p)}$ cutoffs of 0.523 (moderate) and 0.797 (high), with bootstrap 95% intervals [0.455, 0.691] and [0.691, 0.833], respectively.

## B.5 Trip-Purpose Ordering Robustness {#sec-purpose-rank-robustness-appendix .unnumbered}

The diagnostic uses the published purpose-specific destination and home-charging compatibility ratings. All twelve baseline weights are checked against the Stage 3 scoring implementation. Each rating experiment resets the pseudorandom generator to seed 42, perturbs the four behavioural ratings at each purpose, and clips them to [0,1]. Destination and home-charging ratings remain fixed. The amplitudes are 0.05, 0.10 and 0.15. For ranking comparisons only, suitability scores are rounded to 12 decimal places to prevent floating-point differences from separating mathematically equal scores. Scores equal at this precision retain the listed purpose order for top-k membership and are treated as ties in Kendall's $\tau_b$. The underlying suitability weights used in the trip calculations are unchanged. This is a component-level sensitivity experiment, not validation of trip substitution.

The trip-purpose suitability scores combine expert-assigned ordinal ratings (@tbl-trip-purpose-inputs) through fixed aggregation weights (@eq-trip-purpose-weight). Grid 6 evaluates a fourteen-purpose specification with directly assigned charging-flexibility ratings, giving a commuting suitability weight of 0.8575 under the 0.35/0.35/0.30 weighting scheme. The analysis in this section evaluates the twelve-purpose Stage 3 specification, including its composite charging-flexibility calculation, which gives a commuting weight of 0.8335. To test whether the purpose ordering rests on either choice, two further experiments were run: (i) the three top-level aggregation weights were varied over a restricted simplex in 0.05 steps, with each weight constrained to 0.10--0.80 and the three weights summing to one, giving 120 schemes, of which 19 lie within $\pm 0.10$ of the reference 0.35/0.35/0.30 scheme and constitute the plausible alternatives; and (ii) the 12 $\times$ 4 ordinal ratings were jointly perturbed with independent uniform noise at three amplitudes, with 10,000 Monte Carlo draws per amplitude. The destination-infrastructure and home-charging terms are held at the configured purpose-specific compatibility ratings; the experiment varies the stated behavioural ratings and aggregation weights. @tbl-purpose-rank-robustness reports the share of variants in which the baseline top and bottom of the ordering are preserved, together with the median Kendall rank correlation. Commuting and education remain the top-two set under plausible weight schemes or $\pm 0.05$ rating jitter, and the top three purposes are preserved in 94.7% and 80.8% of those variants respectively. Stability declines for the lowest-ranked purposes and under implausibly broad perturbations, so substantive interpretation rests on the rank order of the leading purposes rather than on the precise score of any single purpose.

| Experiment | Variants | Top-1 | Top-2 | Top-3 | Bottom-2 | Median $\tau$-b |
|--------------------------------------------------|:-------------:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:--------:|:---------------:|
| Aggregation weights, plausible ($\pm 0.10$) | 19 schemes | 100% | 100% | 94.7% | 84.2% | 0.97 |
| Aggregation weights, restricted simplex | 120 schemes | 95.8% | 92.5% | 69.2% | 62.5% | 0.91 |
| Rating jitter, $\pm 0.05$ | 10,000 draws | 95.2% | 100% | 80.8% | 79.1% | 0.97 |
| Rating jitter, $\pm 0.10$ | 10,000 draws | 78.6% | 99.5% | 66.3% | 55.5% | 0.91 |
| Rating jitter, $\pm 0.15$ | 10,000 draws | 68.4% | 92.3% | 59.2% | 39.1% | 0.85 |
: Robustness of the trip-purpose suitability ordering to alternative aggregation-weight schemes and to random perturbation of the expert-assigned ordinal ratings. Cell values give the share of variants in which the baseline top-k (or bottom-2) set of purposes is retained, and the median tie-corrected Kendall rank correlation against the baseline ordering. {#tbl-purpose-rank-robustness}

## B.6 Trip-Chaining Sensitivity {#sec-chaining-sensitivity .unnumbered}

The chaining scenarios in @tbl-chaining-bound use $S_{adj}=S_0-E\phi S_H$, with $S_0=\sum N_{ij}^{(p)}/\sum f_{ij}^{(p)}$ and $S_H=\sum N_{ij}^{(p)}\mathbf{1}\{H_i=1,d_{ij}\leq40\}/\sum f_{ij}^{(p)}$. The same unrounded denominator and purpose weights are used throughout. The reference theoretical share is `r r2_pct(r2_metrics$potential_volume)`%, while the affected home-chargeable subset contributes `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*r2_home_share)` percentage points. Public-chargeable short trips and medium-distance trips remain outside this home-only round-trip diagnostic.
The exposure assumptions are informed by the Department for Transport's ad-hoc National Travel Survey trip-chaining analysis (NTSQ09078, England 2024) [@DfTTripChaining2024]. Exposure is varied from 0.23 to 0.29 as a transferred sensitivity assumption. This range depends on arrival-leg versus either-leg attribution and the purpose composition used in its supporting derivation. The failure fraction is varied independently from 0.25 to one, and every trip outside $S_H$ is held unchanged.
For the affected subset, each home-to-stop distance satisfies $d_j\leq40$ km. The same-corridor limiting case assumes that both stops lie on one shared route from home, with symmetric outward and return travel and no additional detours. Under these assumptions, $T=2\max(d_1,d_2)\le80$ km. Geographical alignment alone does not establish this route structure, and the construction does not estimate failure on actual chained road journeys. Their length also depends on the inter-stop and return routes, which this diagnostic does not reconstruct. In the idealised opposed case, $T=2(d_1+d_2)$ and range exceedance occurs when $d_1+d_2>40$ km. Its failure fraction is computed from independent, purpose-volume-weighted partner draws within each RTP. The resulting failure fractions range from `r r2_opposed_range`\% across all seven RTPs (SWESTRANS to ZetTrans). Weighting the regional failure fractions by their eligible home-subset volumes gives `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*r2_opposed_national)`\% nationally. These values describe the synthetic routed-trip population under the assumed pairing. The failure grid in @tbl-chaining-bound is an independently specified stress test.
The tour diagnostic assumes no en-route or destination recharging before returning home. For fixed routes and usable battery range, this is conservative with respect to charging opportunities because feasible intermediate recharging could reduce range failures. At $E=0.29$ and $\phi=1$, the scenario yields `r sprintf("%.1f", r2_chain_floor)`\% theoretical potential. The conditional minimum holds trips outside the selected subset fixed. Asymmetric routes, actual destination pairing and multiple tours per day remain outside this diagnostic, which is evaluated separately from the AP, decay and purpose scenarios.

## B.7 Demographic Transitions and Observed-Market Alignment {#sec-ap-threshold-study .unnumbered}

The threshold study holds the reference adoption-propensity surface fixed and examines all 46,359 Output Areas. Household-weighted models describe car availability, social-grade composition, accommodation and home-charging feasibility. Local two-line models allow a level and slope change within fixed AP windows of 0.15--0.45 and 0.65--0.95, scanning candidate boundaries in 0.01 steps. Separate continuous models scan one or two slope changes across 0.05--0.95 in 0.025 steps and are compared with linear, quadratic and fixed 0.30/0.80 specifications. Leave-one-RTP-out comparisons select boundaries within the training regions. These demographic changes describe the components used to construct AP.
Local demographic changes cluster near 0.29 at the lower edge. Across the broad bands, low AP is associated with lower car ownership and charging readiness. Immediately around 0.30, however, social-grade and housing composition change in different directions: the 0.30--0.35 group has more ABC1 residents but also more flats and car-free households than the 0.25--0.30 group. The boundary marks a transition in demographic composition. Upper local changes occur near 0.76--0.82 for four indicators, with the no-car outcome changing nearer 0.89. @tbl-ap-local-transitions reports both fitted locations and their omitted-region ranges.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ap-local-transitions
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Local demographic transition locations. Ranges show training-sample selections when each RTP is omitted, not confidence intervals. Local samples are fixed before scanning each boundary."
ap_local_lower <- ap_local[ap_local$edge == "lower", ]
ap_local_upper <- ap_local[ap_local$edge == "upper", ]
stopifnot(identical(ap_local_lower$outcome, ap_local_upper$outcome))
ap_local_display <- data.frame(
    Indicator = c("No car/van", "Two or more cars/vans", "ABC1 share", "Flatted accommodation", "Home-charging score"),
    Lower = sprintf("%.2f", ap_local_lower$best_threshold),
    `Lower range` = sprintf("%.2f--%.2f", ap_local_lower$fold_threshold_min, ap_local_lower$fold_threshold_max),
    Upper = sprintf("%.2f", ap_local_upper$best_threshold),
    `Upper range` = sprintf("%.2f--%.2f", ap_local_upper$fold_threshold_min, ap_local_upper$fold_threshold_max),
    check.names = FALSE
)
r2_full_width_table(ap_local_display, font_size = 9)
```

The house-price comparison uses numeric 2022 Data-Zone median sale prices with at least five transactions, and ambiguous duplicate zone-year keys are excluded. The fitted single slope change in log price occurs at AP = `r sprintf("%.3f", ap_stat("log_price", "estimated_one", "lower"))`, but omitted-region estimates span `r sprintf("%.3f--%.3f", ap_stat("log_price", "estimated_one", "fold_lower_min"), ap_stat("log_price", "estimated_one", "fold_lower_max"))`. A complementary private-BEV stock comparison uses observed DfT 2025 Q4 counts in `r format(ap_study_manifest$observed_bev_datazones, big.mark=",")` of 7,392 Data Zones. Absent or suppressed counts are not treated as zero. Its single change occurs at `r sprintf("%.3f", ap_stat("bev_rate", "estimated_one", "lower"))`, with omitted-region estimates of `r sprintf("%.3f--%.3f", ap_stat("bev_rate", "estimated_one", "fold_lower_min"), ap_stat("bev_rate", "estimated_one", "fold_lower_max"))`. These checks provide anchors near the reference edges, although global two-break models and different outcomes select other locations.

![Demographic and house-price gradients, and lower-price MOT threshold sensitivity. Panels (a) and (b) show household-weighted OA profiles in 0.025 AP bins; panel (c) shows the median and interquartile range of Data-Zone median house prices in 0.05 bins. Dashed lines mark 0.30 and 0.80. Panel (d) reports leave-one-postcode-area-out error at each fixed candidate band, controlling for log mean house price; the white cross marks the reference. Selection-adjusted errors are reported separately in the table below.](figures/threshold_evidence.png){#fig-ap-threshold-evidence width=100%}
The MOT comparison uses 11,348 deduplicated electric-coded passing-MOT vehicles first used in 2019--2020, of which 10,802 have price matches. Premium denotes a model-price proxy exceeding 1.5 times the annualised weekly-earnings reference in the first-use year. The April UK median gross weekly earnings for full-time employee jobs are rounded to £585 for 2019 and £586 for 2020 [@ONSASHE2025Earnings]. Multiplication by 52 gives references of £30,420 and £30,472, with strict premium thresholds of £45,630 and £45,708, respectively. These annualised weekly references differ from median annual earnings and from household disposable income. One supplied OA centroid assigns each area to at most one postcode polygon, yielding 16 postcode areas, and the retained main-text price-segment plots use the 14-area sample inherited from the 2011--2022 comparison, whose 2011 MOT count support excludes HS and ZE. The threshold study models lower-price vehicles per 1,000 households and the premium fraction among price-matched vehicles, using household-normalised AP sums and log 2019--2020 mean sale price as a wealth control. This separates area size from market composition. Nested leave-one-postcode-area-out comparisons select among 225 lower-price bands or 15 premium upper edges within each training sample.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ap-mot-cross-validation
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Internal postcode-area prediction checks with a log-house-price control (16 areas). Lower-price RMSE is vehicles per 1,000 households; premium RMSE is percentage points of the price-matched sample. CV R2 compares omitted-area errors with variation around the overall outcome mean; negative values indicate poor predictive performance. Threshold selection is nested within each training sample."
ap_cv_models <- c("controls_only", "fixed", "nested_selected", "continuous_ap")
ap_cv_lower <- ap_mot_cv[ap_mot_cv$segment == "lower_price" & ap_mot_cv$control == "house_price", ]
ap_cv_premium <- ap_mot_cv[ap_mot_cv$segment == "premium" & ap_mot_cv$control == "house_price", ]
ap_cv_lower <- ap_cv_lower[match(ap_cv_models, ap_cv_lower$model), ]
ap_cv_premium <- ap_cv_premium[match(ap_cv_models, ap_cv_premium$model), ]
ap_cv_display <- data.frame(
    Model = c("House price only", "Reference edges", "Selected edges", "Continuous AP"),
    `Lower RMSE` = ap_cv_lower$rmse,
    `Lower CV R2` = ap_cv_lower$r2,
    `Premium RMSE` = 100 * ap_cv_premium$rmse,
    `Premium CV R2` = ap_cv_premium$r2,
    check.names = FALSE
)
r2_full_width_table(ap_cv_display, digits = 3, font_size = 9)
```

Raw count associations remain strong, but household-normalised results are more selective. The reference lower-price band does not improve omitted-area prediction over house price alone. Its CV $R^2$ is `r sprintf("%.3f", ap_cv_lower$r2[2])`. For the premium fraction, the reference upper edge gives CV $R^2$ = `r sprintf("%.3f", ap_cv_premium$r2[2])`, compared with `r sprintf("%.3f", ap_cv_premium$r2[3])` when the upper edge is selected within training areas. Selected edges lie at 0.900--0.925. Thus 0.30 and 0.80 summarise demographic transition regions for the reference affordability-oriented scenario. These internal conventional-BEV checks remain conditional on the fixed reference AP score. The paired screened/unscreened results in @tbl-demographic-screen and the alternative-band outcomes in @tbl-band-edge-headline report the implications for substitution volumes.
